contract_review.settlement_definition: After the reconciliation this archetype holds four series: KXNBAPTS (single-game player points N+), KXNBALADDERPTS (points ladder), KXNBAPTSPROT (protected points) and KXNBABENCHPTS (bench points, apparently a team's non-starter total). Rules are sampled for KXNBAPTS and KXNBAPTSPROT: YES if the named player records N+ points (floor_strike N-0.5) in the named game. The KXNBAPTS text settles an inactive player, or one active but never taking the court, at a fair price, and once he enters on his recorded points; the sampled KXNBAPTSPROT secondary text is cut off after the protection clause, so its inactive and postponement wording is assumed to match KXNBAPTS, not read. The protected variant additionally resolves at the pre-tip fair price when the player enters in the first half but not after it (including any overtime period), unless he already has the required points. Postponed games starting within 48 hours stay open, otherwise all markets resolve at a fair price (KXNBAPTS text). KXNBALADDERPTS and KXNBABENCHPTS are TITLE_ONLY; overtime inclusion (not stated in either sampled text) and the bench definition are unverified.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official box-score points as reported by the 'Source Agencies' referred to in the full rules; the sampled KXNBAPTS text is truncated before naming them. Bench classification would come from the official starter flag (unverified for KXNBABENCHPTS).
variants_and_edge_cases: Standard ladder (KXNBAPTS, rules-verified; KXNBALADDERPTS assumed the same): rungs are nested events P(points >= N), so the fitted curve must be monotone in N; inactive or never-entering players are voided at a fair price, while an early exit after entering settles on actual points.

Protected points (KXNBAPTSPROT, rules-verified): a first-half-only appearance is refunded at the pre-tip fair price unless the strike is already met; the pre-tip fair price already embeds P(early exit), so the protected fair value is not the standard rung conditioned on playing the second half.

Bench points (KXNBABENCHPTS): if it settles on a team's non-starter points, the starting-lineup announcement defines who counts as bench, blowouts raise bench minutes for both teams, and a scratched starter both promotes a reserve out of the bench pool and adds minutes to it; the direction of most drivers is opposite to the star ladders.

Overtime: neither the KXNBAPTS nor the KXNBAPTSPROT text says whether ordinary-ladder points include overtime (the protected text mentions overtime only as part of 'after the conclusion of the first half'); official final box scores normally include OT, which adds about five minutes for starters in roughly 6% of games (pp-ot-inclusion).

player_rebounds.label: NBA player rebounds over/under ladder
player_rebounds.target: Player rebounds over a strike (typically 4+ to 14+)
player_rebounds.mechanism: Rebounds = minutes x rebound chances per minute x conversion. Chances depend on the number of missed shots in the game (pace and both teams' shooting), where the player stands on the floor (rim vs perimeter), and share competition with other bigs. Opponent shot profile (3PA-heavy produces long rebounds), offensive rebounding strategy and teammate absences redistribute the pool. Blowouts cut starters' minutes and favor bench bigs.

inputs.why: Minutes and foul trouble truncate chances, especially for bigs.
Chances and contest rate are more stable than rebounds.
Expected opponent and own missed shots set the supply.
Rebound share is zero-sum among bigs on the floor.
Absent bigs raise remaining bigs' share, nonlinearly.
3PA-heavy opponents create long rebounds favoring guards/wings.
Opponent rebounds allowed to role, shrunk and opponent-adjusted.
Pace scales the pool for NBA player rebounds over/under ladder.
Drop coverage places bigs near the rim; switching moves bigs away from boards.
Foul trouble for bigs reduces minutes.
Blowout risk cuts starters' minutes.
Own and opponent's frontcourt statuses.
Team-rebound credit and scorer practice differ by arena.
Count distribution and dispersion by role.
Price path and the timing of moves relative to injury-report vintages show what is already priced.
DNP/void and stat-source rules define the settled quantity.
Sportsbook prop line is the strongest prior on the mean and the disagreement is the edge.
Rungs of one player-stat must be consistent; off-curve rungs flag stale or thin quotes.
Realized hit rate by rung and price bucket calibrates any model probability.
Reliability curve by price bucket and side shows how far to shade model probabilities for this market family.
Liquidity rank of the rung scales how much edge to discount for better-arbitraged main lines.
Taker-side prints before moves are a candidate informed-flow signal and set realistic fill assumptions.
Settled values (and their timing) are the labels for calibration and need reconciling with the named stat source.
Post-game stat corrections can flip a rung sitting exactly at the threshold, so settlement timing and source matter.
Contested vs uncontested chance splits and box-out data refine conversion estimates.
Role (rim runner vs perimeter) determines rebound location share.
Close games add intentional-foul possessions and free throws that shift guards' and bigs' stat lines.
Fixes the denominator of the rebound process; bigs in foul-heavy games see a smaller player-creditable pool even when total misses are high.
Turns the unquantified frontcourt competition label into a number and links it to injury-conditioned rotation changes.
Adjusts the side-specific mix (OREB vs DREB) which the pooled rebound total hides; relevant for forwards who crash.
Needed to price KXNBAREBPROT correctly versus KXNBAREB for the same player and strike. Cause split includes whole-second-half blowout rest, which interacts with the ratings-based blowout curve.
Big men are often pulled early in lopsided games, and the second-half-entry rule of the protected variant depends on the same blowout path.

interactions.hypothesis: Rebounds scale with pool times minutes share; a fast, poor-shooting game lifts all rebounders.
Absence of a fellow big raises share more than minutes alone, but also increases foul and fatigue risk.
Opponent three-point-heavy profiles shift rebounds to perimeter players and away from bigs.
Bigs in foul trouble in lopsided games are most likely to see minutes truncated, creating fat left tails.

Expected rebounds equal minutes share times the pool times conversion share, so a fast game of poor shooting multiplies the benefit of a full minutes load; in a blowout the pool is large but the starter is on the bench, leaving the product small.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress rebounds on log pool, log minutes and their product; check that the elasticity of minutes rises with pool size.

interactions.hypothesis: The share a big inherits when another big is absent depends on which player replaces the minutes: a stretch forward replacing a rim-runner gives the survivor extra share, a second center gives little; so the absence effect is conditional on the replacement type, not additive.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate absence effect separately by replacement archetype (big vs wing) with stint data and test equality of effects.

interactions.hypothesis: A team that crashes the offensive glass concedes transition chances and plays slower after its own misses; opponent transition frequency changes pace and the miss supply in subsequent possessions, so crash policy has a nonlinear effect on the pool via pace.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare possession counts per 48 for high-crash vs low-crash teams, controlling for opponent, and relate to OREB totals.

interactions.hypothesis: A big with a high foul rate in a lopsided game is likelier to be benched early in the first half and then not return, producing joint extreme left-tail minutes; the two sources of truncation are not independent because coaches avoid risking a foul-prone starter once the margin is large.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute P(minutes<20) by foul-rate tercile within blowout-probability terciles; test for a non-additive cell.

interactions.hypothesis: A designated or returning big carries a first-half-only appearance hazard; protected contracts refund this branch while standard contracts settle NO, so identical status information has opposite value in the two series.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare realised first-half-only appearances by status vintage and test the resulting price gap between KXNBAREBPROT and KXNBAREB for the same strike.

interactions.hypothesis: For protected rebound contracts a halftime margin beyond about 20 points makes a no-second-half appearance likely for bench bigs but not for starters, so the refund branch probability and the value of the protection depend on the margin path and the player's rotation slot, in opposite directions for the two groups.
interactions.how_to_test: From play-by-play compute P(no second-half minutes | entered first half) by halftime margin bin and by starter or bench status, and compare with the injury-only hazard.

nonlinearities.shape: concave: conversion share saturates as chances rise
nonlinearities.why: Chances above a player's available share increase contested boards, where conversion falls; the marginal rebound per added chance declines, so the mean response flattens for the top rebounders.

nonlinearities.shape: threshold: benching onset at 2 first-half fouls and 4-5 total
nonlinearities.why: Coaches bench bigs on a foul count, so the minutes loss from fouls is a step function of foul count rather than linear in the per-minute foul rate.

nonlinearities.shape: convex in dispersion: rung probability for 10+ rises faster than the mean when the pool variance is high
nonlinearities.why: Because the 10+ threshold sits in the upper tail for most players, doubling pool variance raises tail probability more than a proportional mean shift would.

mechanism_review.summary: Rebounds are minutes times the rate at which missed shots (both teams') land within reach times the share of those the player secures. The chain is: participation and minutes (bigs are foul- and blowout-sensitive), the supply of creditable misses given pace, both teams' shot quality and the free-throw and team-rebound leakage, how that supply splits between offensive and defensive boards given each coach's crash policy, the player's share given which other rebounders are on the floor and where he stands (rim vs perimeter), conversion of chances to rebounds (contested vs uncontested, deferrals), and the distributional consequences: counts are overdispersed because the supply itself varies with shooting luck of both teams, and the shared supply makes teammates' rebound counts negatively dependent. The existing catalog captures supply and share conceptually but not the credit leakage, the lineup-pairing arithmetic or the protected-contract state.

stages.name: Appearance, minutes and foul exposure
stages.description: A big either plays a standard 28-36 minutes or loses time to foul trouble, a blowout, or an injury. Rebounds are strongly minutes-dependent, and bigs pick up early fouls that trigger first-half benching, so the minutes distribution has a heavy left tail. For protected contracts the first-half-only branch has a distinct payoff.
stages.distribution: Minutes mixture with a left-tail mass from fouls and blowouts; foul accumulation is a count process with a coach-specific benching threshold (two early, three in first half).

stages.name: Supply of creditable misses
stages.description: The number of missed shots is the sum of two teams' misses, a function of pace and each side's shot quality; part of the supply is lost to team rebounds, out-of-bounds recoveries and dead free-throw attempts. High-scoring, high-FG% games shrink the pool, while games with bad shooting enlarge it, which makes rebounds negatively correlated with total points.
stages.distribution: Supply approximately normal with sd of about 5-6 misses but with a negative dependence on shooting luck; leakage varies with foul volume.

stages.name: Offensive and defensive split by team strategy
stages.description: Offensive rebounds depend on how many players crash and how the opponent defends the glass; defensive boards depend on the opponent's attack style and whether players leak out in transition. A big on a crashing team has a higher offensive component with more variance. Opponent scheme (drop vs switching) positions centers near or far from the rim.
stages.distribution: OREB count is a thinned process with team-specific rate; DREB dominates the mean but OREB adds right-tail variance.

stages.name: Share among on-court rebounders
stages.description: Given a creditable miss, who secures it depends on position, box-out assignment and the other bigs on the floor. The share is lineup-specific: a center's TRB% is far higher beside four perimeter players than beside another big. Teammate absences reallocate shares to specific survivors, and bench bigs inherit starters' shares only partly.
stages.distribution: Shares are bounded, sum to one across the five on court (negative dependence among teammates); share estimates carry sampling error that depends on possessions together.

stages.name: Count distribution and settlement
stages.description: Conditional on supply and share, the count is overdispersed relative to Poisson and discrete at the strike; rungs near the mean are very sensitive to dispersion. Scorer credit for team rebounds and rare video-review corrections matter only at exact-threshold counts. Settlement uses the official box score with a fair-price refund only for inactive players (or first-half-only in the protected series).
stages.distribution: Negative-binomial-like with dispersion driven by pool variance and minutes mixture; integer counts; rung probabilities concentrated in a 7-12 range.

talent_strength.note: Individual rebounding ability expressed as chances and share per on-court possession, adjusted for pairings.

opponent_matchup.note: Opponent scheme and glass strategy shift where rebounds fall; positional allowance is weak.

role_personnel.note: Zero-sum share among bigs on the floor; the key variable set.

availability_news.note: Own and opposing frontcourt status and the first-half-only hazard needed for the protected variant.

coaching_scheme.note: Crash policy, coverage and rotation choices of both coaches.

environment.note: Venue and altitude influence rebounds only through shooting percentages and fatigue, both of which are small and already reflected in the pool and minutes inputs; no standalone environment variable is warranted for this contract.

game_context_script.note: Blowout minutes loss and late-game foul sequences.

pace_volume.note: Supply of misses and the creditable fraction of it.

efficiency_conversion.note: Conversion of chances to rebounds (contested vs uncontested) and the shooting-percentage side of the pool.

distribution_variance.note: Overdispersion from pool variance and minutes mixture; dependence among teammates through the shared pool.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Back-to-back, minutes ramp-up after injury and clinch-rest decisions change bigs' minutes but are not represented by any input in this archetype's list; rest enters implicitly through projected minutes only.

officiating_rules.note: Scorer credit of team rebounds and the foul-call environment that drives bigs' benching.

settlement_contract.note: Standard vs protected refund logic and the official rebounds count.

contract_review.settlement_definition: Binary ladder on one player's official rebounds in the named game: YES if rebounds are at or above N (floor_strike N-0.5, strike_type greater, titles like '10+ rebounds'). Inactive or never-entering players settle at a fair price; once he enters the market settles on actual rebounds. A postponed game that begins within 48 hours stays open, otherwise all markets resolve at a fair price. The protected variant (KXNBAREBPROT) additionally refunds, at the pre-tip fair price, a player who enters in the first half but not after halftime (including overtime), unless he already has the required rebounds. Both live series (KXNBAREB, KXNBAREBPROT) have sampled rules; neither says whether overtime rebounds count.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official box-score rebounds as named in the full rules (the sampled secondary text is cut before listing source agencies, so the exact source and correction policy are unverified).
variants_and_edge_cases: Protected (KXNBAREBPROT) vs standard (KXNBAREB) on the same player and strike have different payoffs for the same early-exit event; a model must carry both forms.
Sampled strikes include 10+ for a wing (Mario Hezonja, floor_strike 9.5) which is a far-tail rung; ladder rungs span the tail and low-probability rungs are dominated by pool variance not talent.
Overtime is not addressed in the sampled standard text; official box score rebounds normally include OT, adding five minutes of pool in about 6% of games.

Protected refund value: KXNBAREBPROT refunds at 'the fair price prior to the opening tip', a price that already embeds the pre-tip chance of a first-half-only appearance, so the protected contract's fair value is not simply the standard rung conditional on playing the second half.

player_assists.label: NBA player assists over/under ladder
player_assists.target: Player assists over an integer strike (2+ to 12+)
player_assists.mechanism: Assists = potential assists x teammate conversion. Potential assists = minutes x ball-handling and creation rate, scaled by pace and the availability of finishers. Conversion depends on the shot quality and shooting skill of teammates on the floor and on opponent scheme (switching reduces assisted baskets, pressure increases turnovers). Teammate absences change both factors in opposite directions depending on whether the absent player is a creator or a finisher. Blowouts truncate minutes; official-scorer credit adds noise.

Team scoring environment for NBA player assists over/under ladder.

Settled values (and their timing) are the labels for calibration and need reconciling with the named stat source.
Post-game stat corrections can flip a rung sitting exactly at the threshold, so settlement timing and source matter.
Passing and touch tracking supply potential assists and time of possession.

Close games add intentional-foul possessions and free throws that shift guards' and bigs' stat lines.
The product of share and expected team assisted makes gives the mean directly and exposes how teammates' shooting enters.
Replaces a market-derived environment with an own estimate focused on assisted makes, the quantity assists actually count.
Directly addresses 'who else creates', the main role redistribution for assists that teammate absence alone cannot split.

The protected KXNBAASTPROT contract voids a first-half-only appearance (injury or a coach resting the creator through a blowout second half); this input gives P(void) and conditions the settled distribution, and the unprotected KXNBAAST needs only the zero-minute part.
Replaces the spread-based nba.garbage in player_assists: blowout truncation of the relevant players' minutes from own ratings and the coach's pull curve, with no closing line used.

interactions.hypothesis: When the absent teammate was a finisher the star's usage rises but assists can fall because conversion falls; when the absent was a creator assists rise.
Spread x minutes: a guard on a heavy favorite has a lower over probability at high rungs even when his per-minute rate is high.
Potential assists scale with pace only to the degree the player is on the ball in transition; pace effect is role-dependent.
Teammate shooting hot streaks inflate assist counts; regress conversion to talent rather than using recent assist averages.
A switch-heavy opponent reduces assisted baskets for pick-and-roll creators; effect is larger than raw assists-allowed to position suggests.

A missing finisher cuts conversion while potential assists stay constant, a missing creator raises the player's potential assists, so the direction of the absence effect on assists depends on the absent player's role; a single dummy averages opposite effects to zero.
interactions.how_to_test: Split absence games by absent-player role and regress assists on potential assists and teammate shooting separately.

interactions.hypothesis: A lead guard on a heavy favourite loses late minutes, which removes the upper rungs; effect appears beyond a expected margin threshold near 8-10 and concentrates in the 9+ assist rungs.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare P(9+ assists) in expected margin buckets for guards controlling for per-minute rate.

interactions.hypothesis: Potential assists per minute scale with the share of initiations the player owns, so doubling co-creator load roughly halves his share; the effect is multiplicative on the per-minute rate and larger for players who rely on on-ball time.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress log potential assists per minute on log co-creator load with player fixed effects.

interactions.hypothesis: Switch-heavy defences reduce assisted baskets for pick-and-roll creators more than for off-ball movers, so the opponent effect depends on the creator's primary action; ranking by raw assists allowed hides that.
interactions.how_to_test: Interact opponent coverage with the player's pick-and-roll initiation share.

interactions.hypothesis: Teammate shooting luck is common to all of a creator's potential assists in the game, so assists have a variance larger than a binomial with independent makes; this variance is shared with teammates' scoring props.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare residual variance of assists with a binomial benchmark and correlate residuals with team three-point percentage.

nonlinearities.shape: Hinge near a 9-point expected margin, concave after
nonlinearities.why: Minutes for lead ball handlers fall steeply once starters are expected to sit; extra expected margin beyond about 14 changes little since the starters are already out.

nonlinearities.shape: Regression toward talent with a shrinkage weight near 0.6-0.7 for a 10-game sample
nonlinearities.why: Hot team shooting of the last 10 games overstates conversion; the response of future assists to recent conversion is much flatter than one.

nonlinearities.shape: Right-skewed overdispersed with heavier tail for primary creators
nonlinearities.why: A guard with a mean of 7.5 has more mass at 12+ than a Poisson, so high rungs are less steeply priced than a simple model implies.

nonlinearities.shape: Diminishing conversion at high potential-assist counts
nonlinearities.why: When the number of potential assists is very high the marginal pass is lower quality, so assists rise less than proportionally in games with extreme potential assists.

mechanism_review.summary: An assist is credited when a player's pass directly leads to a made field goal by a teammate, so the count is (team made field goals while he is on court) x (share of those baskets he assisted). The first factor depends on how many minutes the player plays, how many possessions the team uses in that time, the team's shooting quality that night and its assisted share (isolation-heavy teams assist less); the second factor depends on his ball-handling role, how many other creators share the floor, and how often a pass becomes an assisted make as opposed to a missed shot, a turnover or an unassisted attack. Variation therefore comes from minutes (blowout and foul truncation), teammates' shooting luck (the largest single-game noise source), lineup composition (who finishes, who else creates) and scorer-credit judgement. The count is overdispersed with a right tail for primary creators, and the discrete threshold at 8+ amplifies small shifts in the mean, so P(N+) is far more sensitive to teammates' shooting variance than to the player's own skill noise.

stages.name: Court time of the creator
stages.description: Assists accrue only on court, so the number of possessions the lead ball handler plays is the opportunity base. Primary creators play 30-36 minutes in normal games but 24-28 when the game is decided, and leave early when injured; the unprotected contract voids only a zero-minute game and the protected one a first-half-only exit. Rest and load-management habits change the starting minutes. For the protected series the early-exit hazard (injury, ejection, or a coach resting the lead guard for the whole second half of a first-half blowout) sets the void probability and the conditional distribution of the settled count.
stages.distribution: Mixture of normal-game, truncated-blowout and early-exit regimes; sd of minutes about 5 for starters, and a point mass at zero minutes that is voided.

stages.name: Ball-handling volume and creation role
stages.description: Per minute, assist chances are produced by time of possession, touches, pick-and-roll initiations and passes; potential assists measure the pass leading to a shot attempt. Role matters: a lead guard might average roughly 10-14 potential assists per game and league-leading creators well into the high teens (recalled, unsourced, u1) while a wing averages 4-6. The presence of a co-creator (another high-usage ball handler) divides the initiations, and a missing co-creator increases the share.
stages.distribution: Potential assists per minute is stable (cross-game sd about 25% of the mean) and approximately Poisson-overdispersed per game.

stages.name: Team scoring environment and assisted-shot share
stages.description: The pool of assistable baskets is the team's made field goals, and the fraction that are assisted varies with style (ball-movement offences about 65-70%, isolation-heavy about 50-55%), shot type (threes and rim finishes are assisted at higher rates than pull-up twos) and the opponent's scheme (switching and pressure reduce clean passing lanes). The expected number of team assisted makes in the player's minutes is the volume he draws from.
stages.distribution: Team assisted FGM per game: mean about 26, sd about 4.5; positively correlated with team field-goal percentage that night.

stages.name: Conversion by teammates on the floor
stages.description: Potential assists become assists only if the teammate makes the shot, so the on-court teammates' shooting skill and shot quality set the conversion; hot or cold shooting from teammates is the largest noise term because a creator has no control over makes. With a major finisher absent, conversion drops even if potential assists stay the same, while with a creator absent the player's potential assists rise.
stages.distribution: Binomial conversion of 10-14 potential assists at p about 0.5-0.6, with additional between-game luck in teammate shooting (sd of about 6-8 percentage points); the product is overdispersed.

stages.name: Credit, distribution and rung probability
stages.description: The official scorer awards the assist by judgement (how many dribbles, whether the pass created the shot), with arena and scorer tendencies that move totals by about half an assist on average, and post-game corrections occasionally change a count. The resulting integer count is right-skewed and the rung probabilities P(N+) follow its survival function, with fair-price voids for non-appearance in the unprotected contract.
stages.distribution: Overdispersed discrete count (negative-binomial-like), variance ratio about 1.3-1.6 for guards, with scorer-level offsets of about 0.3-0.7 assists.

contract_review.settlement_definition: Assist ladder markets settle Yes if the named player records at least N assists (strike 7.5 means 8+) in the single named game, using the player's final recorded assists. Two variants are live: KXNBAAST (unprotected) settles to a fair price if the player is inactive or active but never takes the court, and on actual assists once he enters; KXNBAASTPROT (protected) settles to the pre-tip fair price if the player enters in the first half but not after the first half (including overtime) unless he already has the required assists, and on actual statistics whenever he enters after the first half, regardless of first-half participation. A short postponement stays open; a game cancelled or not started within 48 hours resolves to fair price. Assists are an official-scorer statistic subject to later correction. The sampled KXNBAASTPROT secondary text is truncated at 600 characters in the evidence pack, so any inactive-player and overtime sentences that follow it were never seen.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official league box score assist totals (NBA.com), including later stat corrections.
variants_and_edge_cases: Protected versus unprotected: the same player and threshold can be listed under both tickers with different void sets, so the probabilities of Yes conditional on settlement differ.
Inactive versus active-but-no-minutes: both void at fair price in the unprotected rule, so late scratches affect edge accounting but not the settled count.

Overtime: the protected text mentions overtime only for the second-half-entry test ("including any overtime period"); whether overtime assists count toward the total is not stated in any sampled text and is assumed to follow official box-score totals (u5).
Assist credit is an official scorer judgement and is subject to post-game stat corrections that can flip a rung at the threshold.
Rungs run from 2+ to 12+ for different players; the same distribution should satisfy monotone survival across rungs.

player_threes.label: NBA player threes made over/under ladder
player_threes.target: Player three-pointers made over a strike (1+ to 7+)
player_threes.mechanism: Threes made = attempts x make probability with attempts overdispersed and make probability shrunk heavily to talent; both vary with minutes, role, defensive pressure and shot openness. Opponent scheme (switch, drop, perimeter defense), pace and teammate absences determine attempt volume. Luck dominates make probability in one game, so the pregame edge is mostly in attempt volume and minutes rather than in 3P% trends.

inputs.why: Minutes scale attempts; blowouts reduce them.
3PA per minute and catch-and-shoot share are stable inputs.
Shrink 3P% heavily; recent hot streaks overstate true talent.
Pull-up vs catch-and-shoot role changes attempt volume.
When a primary creator is out, spot-up shooters lose open looks while bench shooters gain minutes.
Opponent 3PA and 3P% allowed to role.
Drop coverage concedes three-point attempts; switching limits them.
Share of shots from three and corner/above-break split.
Possessions scale attempts for NBA player threes made over/under ladder.
Starters lose minutes in blowouts.
Team-level hot/cold shooting regresses toward shot-quality expectation.

Spot-up vs pull-up role determines how attempts respond to absences.

Separates context-driven make probability from luck; the existing regression input shrinks a pooled 3P% instead. Rebased on public per-shot fields so it does not depend on per-shot defender distance; role is secondary until the tracking splits are confirmed.
Captures role-specific blowout asymmetries that make bench shooters better, not worse, in lopsided games.
Translates an injury headline into a number of lost assisted threes for each shooter.
A stable, scheme-based replacement for the noisy position-allowed variable. Depends on team-level aggregate dashboards whose date-window vintages are SOURCE_UNVERIFIED (p3-defender-distance).
Three-point attempts concentrate among starters and fall when starters sit in garbage time, but trailing teams also raise three volume; the margin-path curve separates the two.
Generates the KXNBA3PTPROT refund branch: P(enters in the first half but not after it) from injury/ejection exits and coach-rested second halves; no other input of this archetype models it.

interactions.hypothesis: Attempts per minute times minutes sets the attempts distribution; minute shortfalls matter more than make-rate drift.
Shrinkage weight depends on the number of career attempts; recent 3P% outlier only matters for low-volume shooters.
Losing a rim-pressure creator reduces open catch-and-shoot attempts against help-heavy schemes.
Opponent 3PA allowed matters mostly when the opponent's scheme is extreme; otherwise noise.

Expected threes are minutes times attempt rate times make probability, so minutes swings dominate for bench shooters whose attempt rate is high but whose minutes vary between 8 and 28; the same minutes error costs far more for a 9-attempt-per-36 shooter than a 3-attempt one.
interactions.how_to_test: Decompose variance of threes into minutes, attempt-rate and make-rate components by role using player-game data and test that the minutes share is largest for bench shooters.

interactions.hypothesis: The shrinkage weight on observed 3P% depends on cumulative attempts: a rookie with 150 attempts keeps little of a hot start while a veteran with 3000 attempts keeps most; recent form matters only for the low-attempt sample.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit predictive error of next-game 3P% using recent-form weight interacted with log career attempts and check that weight declines with attempts.

interactions.hypothesis: A shooter's loss from an absent creator equals the share of his assisted attempts that creator generated times the shortfall of replacements; the effect is therefore concentrated in specific pairs rather than being a general absence penalty, and shooters with diversified passers are insulated.
interactions.how_to_test: For shooters with a dominant passer, compare attempts with vs without that passer; for diversified shooters expect near-zero effect.

interactions.hypothesis: In a blowout the favorite's starters leave and bench shooters play expanded minutes with higher attempt rates, while the trailing team's shooters take more late threes; the sign of the effect of margin on threes depends on role, flipping between starters and bench specialists.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate 3PA per minute by margin bin for starters and bench separately; verify opposite slopes.

interactions.hypothesis: Team-level shooting shocks (a hot night for the whole team) correlate the made-three counts of teammates; this does not change marginals but matters for parlays or when the same team's shooters appear on several rungs at once.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute correlation of made-three residuals between teammates over a season and compare with the independence benchmark.

nonlinearities.shape: convex tail: P(5+) rises faster than the mean attempt rate
nonlinearities.why: A threshold of five makes needs about 13 attempts at 36%; small increases in attempt rate move tail probability multiplicatively because 5+ sits far above the mean.

nonlinearities.shape: saturating: weight on recent make rate declines with attempt count
nonlinearities.why: Bayesian shrinkage gives a weight n/(n+k) on observed rate; with k near 750 attempts the weight on a 100-attempt sample is under 12%, so predicted make probability barely moves.

nonlinearities.shape: non-monotone in margin: attempts fall for starters, rise for bench and trailing team
nonlinearities.why: The effect of blowout probability on threes depends on role and on late-game urgency, giving a U- or inverted-U relation rather than a monotone one.

mechanism_review.summary: Made threes equal attempts times make probability. Attempts are minutes times a per-minute rate set by role (catch-and-shoot spot-up vs on-ball creator), the team's pace and who passes to him, modified by the score path (trailing teams launch more, leading teams bench shooters). Make probability is a context-weighted talent estimate (open catch-and-shoot vs contested pull-up) that is overwhelmingly noise in a single game, so the predictable component is attempts, and the make count is a thinned process whose variance exceeds a plain binomial because attempts and team-level shooting form are random. Settlement is the official count on single-game ladders and protected rungs. The main modelling hazards are role-specific minutes volatility for bench shooters and the dependence between a shooter's attempts and a specific passer's availability.

stages.name: Participation and minutes for a role player
stages.description: Spot-up shooters are often rotation players whose minutes change sharply with matchup, injury news and blowouts, so the minutes distribution is wide and sometimes zero-inflated for players on the edge of the rotation. Once he enters, the contract settles on his count, so brief appearances produce zero or one make.
stages.distribution: Wide mixture, zero- or low-inflated for fringe rotation players; bench minutes weakly dependent on game margin.

stages.name: Attempt rate given role and teammates
stages.description: Three-point attempts per minute reflect the shooter's role: off-ball spot-up players take 7-10 per 36 minutes mostly from passes, on-ball creators take pull-ups. The rate depends on who passes to him (passer availability) and who competes for the same looks, and on the team's pace and style. Attempt counts are overdispersed relative to Poisson because role and game flow change within games.
stages.distribution: Overdispersed count with variance exceeding mean (dispersion index about 1.3-1.8); mean attempt rate shifts by specific teammate absences.

stages.name: Defensive scheme and shot openness
stages.description: The opponent's scheme sets how many attempts are open or contested: drop coverage concedes above-the-break openings, switching and aggressive closeouts reduce them, and blitzing creates kick-out threes for the shooters. Openness affects both attempt volume and per-shot make probability, and it is a scheme trait rather than a luck outcome.
stages.distribution: Categorical scheme effect on both the attempt rate and per-shot make probability; effects of a few percentage points on make probability, 10-20% on attempts.

stages.name: Make probability: talent versus luck
stages.description: Given attempt context, each shot is a Bernoulli trial with probability depending on shot type and openness; single-game make rates are overwhelmingly luck and require heavy shrinkage (hundreds of attempts of prior). Team-level shooting form creates positive correlation across a team's shooters within a game, while player-level hot hands are statistically elusive.
stages.distribution: Sum of heterogeneous Bernoulli trials; per-game variance close to binomial with p near 0.36 plus a team-level shared shock; shrinkage weight depends on attempts.

stages.name: Game script effects on attempts
stages.description: Trailing teams take more threes late in the game and bench shooters gain minutes in blowouts, while starters who sit lose attempts; close games push closers to higher minutes. The net effect on a given shooter depends on role and on the margin path, which makes simple blowout penalties wrong for bench specialists.
stages.distribution: Path-dependent: attempt rate per minute is a function of margin bin and quarter; mixture over projected margin paths.

stages.name: Settlement form
stages.description: The ladder and protected forms are thresholds on one game's count, nested across rungs so the curve must be monotone; the protected form (KXNBA3PTPROT text) removes the first-half-only branch unless the strike is already met, so its value differs from the standard rung exactly in the early-exit scenarios, whose weight is nba.early_exit_hazard (injury exits plus a coach-rested second half). Low rungs depend mostly on the probability of at least one attempt and minutes, high rungs on the attempt tail and shooting luck.
stages.distribution: Integer count per game (mixture of binomials over attempts); protected rungs replace the first-half-exit mass by the pre-tip price.

talent_strength.note: Shooting skill by context with heavy shrinkage; team strength is secondary.

opponent_matchup.note: Scheme and openness allowed matter more than opponent 3P% allowed.

role_personnel.note: Role, passers and competing shooters determine attempts.

availability_news.note: Own status and passer/creator status by vintage, plus the first-half-only participation hazard that the protected series refunds.

coaching_scheme.note: Offensive spacing and rotation decisions plus opponent coverage choice.

environment.note: Arena and altitude effects on three-point percentage are small and unreliable once shooter talent is shrunk; the mechanism for a single game is dominated by attempts and noise, so no separate environment variable is justified.

game_context_script.note: Margin-path dependence of attempts by role.

pace_volume.note: Possessions and per-minute attempt rate.

efficiency_conversion.note: Context-specific make probability and luck regression.

distribution_variance.note: Mixture over attempts with team-level shooting shocks.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Rest-day effects on shooting legs and minutes, and rest-for-seeding decisions for rotation players, have no input in this archetype; second-night-of-back-to-back shooting effect on makes is unmeasured here.

officiating_rules.note: Officials influence threes only through foul calls on shooters (rare) and no official scorer discretion is involved in a made-three count; the contract needs no officiating variable beyond settlement text.

settlement_contract.note: Ladder and protected forms are rules-verified (KXNBA3PT, KXNBA3PTPROT); the ladder series KXNBALADDER3PT is TITLE_ONLY.

contract_review.settlement_definition: Binary ladder: YES if the named player makes at least N three-pointers (floor_strike N-0.5, e.g. 5+ with floor 4.5) in the named game. Per the KXNBA3PT text, inactive or never-entering players settle at a fair price; once he enters, the market settles on actual made threes; postponed games that start within 48 hours stay open, otherwise all markets resolve at a fair price (the KXNBA3PTPROT sample is cut off after its protection clause, so these clauses are assumed, not read, for it). KXNBA3PT and KXNBA3PTPROT have sampled rules; the protected variant resolves at the pre-tip fair price when a player enters in the first half but not after it (including overtime) unless he already has the required threes. KXNBALADDER3PT is TITLE_ONLY. Neither sampled text says whether overtime makes count for the standard ladder.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official box score made three-pointers as named in the full rules; the sampled secondary text is truncated before naming source agencies, so the exact source is unverified.
variants_and_edge_cases: Ladder rungs: only 5+ rungs (KXNBA3PT and KXNBA3PTPROT, floor_strike 4.5) are sampled; a 1+ to 7+ span is assumed from the ladder titles and is not verified from rules text. Low rungs would depend mostly on attempts>=1 and minutes, high rungs on the attempt tail and shooting luck, so key drivers would differ by rung.
Protected (KXNBA3PTPROT, rules-verified): a first-half-only appearance is refunded at the pre-tip fair price unless the strike is met; any appearance after halftime puts it back on actual makes.
Overtime is not addressed in the sampled text; official box score made threes normally include OT, adding about five minutes of attempts in about 6% of games.
Ladder series (KXNBALADDER3PT, TITLE_ONLY): assumed to be the same nested 'N+' rungs as KXNBA3PT, so cross-rung monotonicity must hold, but its void rule is not read.

combo_props.label: NBA combo props (PRA, PR, PA, RA)
combo_props.target: Combined player points+rebounds+assists (or subset) over a strike
combo_props.mechanism: A combo is a sum of correlated components; the mean is the sum of marginal means, while the variance depends on within-game covariance (minutes positive, role tradeoffs negative). Mispricing arises when a market prices combos as independent sums of the component lines, or when component prices update at different speeds after news. All single-stat drivers apply, with minutes and game script as common factors that dominate the tails.

inputs.why: Common multiplier across all components.
Points/assist trade-off and creation role.
Within-game covariance determines the width of the combined distribution.
Marginal shape per component for NBA combo props (PRA, PR, PA, RA).
Redistribution moves points, rebounds and assists in different directions.
Rebound component for NBA combo props (PRA, PR, PA, RA).
Assist component for NBA combo props (PRA, PR, PA, RA).
Scoring component quality for NBA combo props (PRA, PR, PA, RA).
Blowout minutes loss cuts all components together.
Possessions scale the sum for NBA combo props (PRA, PR, PA, RA).
Status of player and teammates.
Team scoring environment for NBA combo props (PRA, PR, PA, RA).
Price path and the timing of moves relative to injury-report vintages show what is already priced.
DNP/void and stat-source rules define the settled quantity.
Sportsbook prop line is the strongest prior on the mean and the disagreement is the edge.
Rungs of one player-stat must be consistent; off-curve rungs flag stale or thin quotes.
Realized hit rate by rung and price bucket calibrates any model probability.
Reliability curve by price bucket and side shows how far to shade model probabilities for this market family.
Liquidity rank of the rung scales how much edge to discount for better-arbitraged main lines.
Taker-side prints before moves are a candidate informed-flow signal and set realistic fill assumptions.
Settled values (and their timing) are the labels for calibration and need reconciling with the named stat source.
Post-game stat corrections can flip a rung sitting exactly at the threshold, so settlement timing and source matter.
A PRA rung's probability is dominated by P(full minutes), which the market prices with a single projected minute number.
Protected PRA contracts void on first-half-only participation, which includes coach-rested second halves, so the void probability must be modelled separately from injury status.
A 'missing teammate' flag cannot tell whether PRA rises (scoring/assist boost) or just redistributes (points up, assists down).
The environment is needed independent of the market price; using spread-implied points would make the model a function of its own benchmark.

Return-from-injury minute restrictions and coach-announced rest set the restriction branch of the minutes mixture; the record's own minutes mixture lists a coach-announced restriction regime that needs this input.
Back-to-back, rest days and travel change star minutes and the probability of load-managed rest; shifts the weights of the minutes scenarios.
Crew foul tendency changes free-throw points, foul trouble (minutes clipped) and pace; used only as a secondary driver of the points and minutes components.
Official-scorer and arena credit bias moves assists, and to a lesser extent rebounds, at the boundary of a three-stat sum; referenced in stage s4 and now attached.
Teammates' conversion of the player's passes sets assists per potential assist; referenced in stage s4 and coverage and now attached.
Replaces the spread-based nba.garbage in combo_props: blowout truncation of the relevant players' minutes from own ratings and the coach's pull curve, with no closing line used.

interactions.hypothesis: Minutes volatility induces positive covariance between components, widening the tails of the combo relative to independent sums.
For creators, scoring and assist usage trade off; combo variance can be smaller than the sum of single-stat variances.
Combo right tail (high rung) depends on blowout probability more than the mean; model with scenario mixture.
With a big out, a wing's rebounds can rise while scoring is unchanged; component-level updates are not uniform.

Expected opportunities are the product of minutes and per-minute volume, but the usage rate itself is lower in garbage minutes, so the product within the blowout regime is much smaller than average minutes times average usage.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate regime-specific usage and compare predicted sums with the naive product on historical games stratified by final margin.

interactions.hypothesis: With the primary creator off court, points and assists move in opposite directions for the scorer-passer while points and rebounds move together for a big, so the covariance sign by component pair flips with the lineup.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute component correlations in on/off splits and test whether the sd of the sum differs from the pooled estimate.

interactions.hypothesis: Past a expected margin of about 10 points the probability of a truncated-minutes game rises steeply, creating a regime switch in the upper rungs while the lower rungs barely move.
interactions.how_to_test: Bucket own-model expected margin and measure P(S>=strike) by rung across expected margin buckets; look for a knee near 9-12 points.

interactions.hypothesis: A questionable teammate's resolution changes the player's usage and assists, and since the protected clause treats the player's own exit separately, the sequence of reports matters: the teammate's status effect is conditional on the player's status being active.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare PRA outcomes by teammate status vintage (listed out before 5pm vs after) controlling for own minutes.

interactions.hypothesis: A protected contract voids a first-half exit, so P(Yes | not void) is a conditional on survival to the second half, shifting probability up for high-hazard players relative to the unprotected equivalent.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare realised hit rates of protected versus unprotected series once voided contracts are removed.

nonlinearities.shape: Knee at |expected margin| near 10, concave beyond
nonlinearities.why: Minutes loss rises slowly for small expected margins and then accelerates as the favourite pulls starters, so the effect on a high rung is convex in the expected margin up to the knee and then saturates.

nonlinearities.shape: Non-Gaussian multimodal with an OT spike
nonlinearities.why: Minutes in the three regimes are 24, 35 and 42 rather than one bell curve; the sum's upper tail is generated mainly by the OT/competitive regime.

nonlinearities.shape: Diminishing returns in points per extra shot
nonlinearities.why: Higher usage reduces efficiency, so doubling shot share does not double points, which flattens the points component for stars.

nonlinearities.shape: Right-skewed integer sum with overdispersion
nonlinearities.why: Count components are overdispersed; the three-component sum has a heavier right tail than a normal with the same sd.

mechanism_review.summary: A combo prop settles on S = PTS + REB + AST over the minutes the player is on court, so the outcome is the sum of three count processes that share one multiplier (minutes) and one environment (possessions) but compete for the same player-level resources. The chain is: does he play and for how long (a mixture over full-length, blowout-truncated, foul-limited and early-exit scenarios), how many team possessions occur in those minutes, which share of them runs through him as shooter, passer or rebounder, how efficiently each opportunity converts, and how the discrete sum lands relative to a half-point threshold. Components are positively correlated through minutes and pace but negatively through role allocation (a creator who scores more shoots instead of assisting; a perimeter-oriented big rebounds fewer), so the variance of the sum is not the sum of variances. The protected clause removes the early-exit lower tail, while overtime and close games add a right tail. Points carry most of the variance, rebounds the least.

stages.name: Participation and protected-state
stages.description: The first gate is whether the player appears. The unprotected KXNBAPRA rule voids inactive or never-on-court players at fair price and settles on actual stats once the player enters, while the protected contract voids a first-half-only appearance unless the strike is already met. So the probability mass is cut at 'minutes = 0' and at 'exit before the halftime return', and what settles on actual stats is either a second-half (or overtime) entry or a first-half-only appearance in which the strike was already reached. Late scratches (inactive 30 minutes before tip), minute restrictions on return and in-game injuries all shape the cut and arrive from official reports and reporter posts at different times. The sampled protected text voids any first-half-only appearance, so the cut includes second halves a coach rests the player through in a first-half blowout, not only injuries, and the text does not say whether being on the floor at the start of the third quarter counts as entering after the first half.
stages.distribution: Spike at zero (void) plus a thin early-exit spike; remaining mass is a continuous minutes distribution. Conditional on playing, the probability of an in-game exit is a small hazard per minute, higher for players with recent injuries.

stages.name: Minutes scenario mixture
stages.description: Minutes are not one number: a starter on a team projected to win by 14 faces a high probability of a 26-minute night, in a competitive game he plays 36, and with foul trouble he is clipped at 28 and then returns. The scenarios mix with different weights depending on expected margin, coach rotation habits and bench quality, and each scenario has its own stat rate because garbage-time minutes are low-usage. OT adds a fixed block of minutes in roughly one game in sixteen.
stages.distribution: Multimodal mixture (blowout 22-28, normal 32-38, OT 40+) rather than a normal; sd of minutes for starters about 5 and sharply state-dependent, tail truncated at 48+5k.

stages.name: Opportunity volume per minute
stages.description: Per minute, the player has shot attempts and free-throw trips (usage), rebound chances (position of shots and team missed shots in his zone), and potential assists (touches and passes). These depend on pace of the game and on which teammates share the floor: missing the primary creator raises usage but also changes who receives the passes. Rebound chances depend on both teams' miss rates and the number of bigs on court.
stages.distribution: Overdispersed counts per minute; opportunity totals are roughly negative-binomial with a variance that grows with team pace variability and lineup churn.

stages.name: Conversion and luck
stages.description: Points are a conversion of attempts (efficiency with high short-window noise on threes), rebounds convert chances at a rate dominated by position and opponent miss quality, assists convert potential assists at teammate shooting rate and the scorer's credit behaviour. Of the three, points carry the largest luck variance in a single game and assist conversion depends on whether teammates are hot; rebounds are comparatively stable. These conversion terms are partly independent, which softens the covariance of the sum.
stages.distribution: Points: binomial-like per attempt with extra shooting-luck variance; assists: binomial on potential assists with arena credit noise; rebounds: close to Poisson given chances. Sum of three non-identical overdispersed counts.

stages.name: Joint distribution and threshold
stages.description: The settled event is the sum crossing an integer line, so the covariance between components matters for the tails: minutes and pace give a positive common factor while role-share gives a negative one, and the net sign depends on the player type (a scoring wing versus a point-guard creator versus a centre). A scenario mixture on minutes plus component-specific residuals produces a right-skewed sum whose mass at the line depends on the mean and the sd.
stages.distribution: Right-skewed integer distribution with sd roughly 6-8 for a star at a mean near 30; the cumulative mass at the rung depends on scenario weights, not just the mean.

talent_strength.note: Player-level production rates are the ability layer for each component.

opponent_matchup.note: Opponent allowed points/rebounds/assists to position; nba.opp_def_pos exists in the catalog but is not attached to this archetype.

role_personnel.note: Who shares the floor changes shot, pass and rebound opportunities in different directions.

availability_news.note: Own and teammates' status plus in-game exit hazard feed the protected-state cut.

coaching_scheme.note: Rotation and garbage-time pull timing decide the minute scenario weights.

environment.note: Altitude, arena and weather act on a single player-game only through possessions and fatigue, which the pace and rest inputs capture; no separate environmental input would add information for a points+rebounds+assists sum.

game_context_script.note: Spread/total environment drives minutes truncation and team scoring.

contract_review.settlement_definition: The sampled live series (KXNBAPRAPROT, a protected points+rebounds+assists contract) settles Yes if the named player records at least the 'N+' combined total (strike 24.5 means 25+) in the single named game. The protected clause converts the contract to the fair price prior to the opening tip when the player enters during the first half but never again after halftime (including overtime) and has not already reached the required total; a player who enters after the first half settles on actual stats regardless of first-half participation. The sampled text is silent on whether overtime stats count in the total, so inclusion is inferred from official box-score practice, not verified. Postponement within 48 hours stays open; otherwise it resolves to fair price. The unprotected KXNBAPRA text (now sampled) voids at fair price only an inactive or never-on-court player and settles on recorded stats once he enters; KXNBAPR and KXNBAPA remain TITLE_ONLY.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official league box score (NBA.com game box score) for points, rebounds and assists; the protected clause uses substitution/play-by-play records to determine first-half entry and second-half entry.
variants_and_edge_cases: Protected versus unprotected: both PRA variants now have sampled rules. KXNBAPRA (unprotected) voids at fair price only if the player is inactive or never takes the court and otherwise settles on actual stats; KXNBAPRAPROT also voids a first-half-only appearance. KXNBAPR and KXNBAPA are TITLE_ONLY, so their DNP wording is assumed, not seen.
Early-exit void: a player who plays the first half and is hurt at halftime produces a fair-price settlement rather than No, which removes the lower tail that otherwise exists.
Strike on a half point: floor_strike 24.5 with 'N+' means a total of exactly 24 is No and 25 is Yes; the integer sum of three counts has no push.
Overtime: the sampled rule text does not say overtime statistics are included; box-score totals normally include them, adding 5 minutes to starters in about 6% of games.
Stat corrections after the game by the league's scorer can alter an assist or rebound and flip a boundary result.

Void value is circular for expected-value work: the protected void pays "the fair price prior to the opening tip", a market-derived reference that exists only once the market has been priced, so evaluate P(settles on actual stats) and P(void) separately and treat the void payout as exogenous.

The text does not say whether a starter "enters" at the tip or at the start of the third quarter, and a first-half starter rested for the whole second half in a blowout (not an injury) is void on the literal wording unless the strike was already reached.

steals_blocks_turnovers.label: NBA steals, blocks, stocks and turnovers
steals_blocks_turnovers.target: Player steals / blocks / stocks / turnovers at 0.5, 1.5, 2.5 strikes
steals_blocks_turnovers.mechanism: These are low-count events with per-minute rates that are stable but with large sampling noise; thresholds at 0.5/1.5 make the outcome very sensitive to dispersion and minutes. Steals depend on opponent turnover-proneness and pace; blocks on opponent rim-attempt volume and own rim-protection role; turnovers on ball-handling load and pressure. Official-scorer credit is a notable noise source. Stocks sum correlated components.

Gives a stabler, scheme-aware rate for the 0.5/1.5/2.5 steal rungs than season steals per minute. Role lowered to secondary: per-game vintages of hustle and rim-defense data are SOURCE_UNVERIFIED (sbt-hustle-access) and may exist only as season aggregates or paid tracking.

Gives the supply side of blocks with the relevant matchup, which pace and total shots miss. Role lowered to secondary: per-game vintages of hustle and rim-defense data are SOURCE_UNVERIFIED (sbt-hustle-access) and may exist only as season aggregates or paid tracking.
Targets the portion of opponent turnovers that a defender can steal.
Provides the dependence parameter needed for KXNBASTOCK that the independent components cannot.
Steals and blocks are low-count events that scale with minutes, so starter minutes lost in a blowout move the mean and the zero mass directly.

interactions.hypothesis: Rate times minutes gives mean; the 0.5 vs 1.5 rung sensitivity to dispersion is higher than to the mean.
Turnovers scale with touches; role change after teammate absence raises turnovers as ball handling load rises.
Blocks track opponent rim attempts more than total FGA; opponent shot profile is a stronger signal than pace.
Scorer credit noise adds extra dispersion that should be included for steals and blocks, not for rebounds.

Mean events equal rate times minutes, but rung probability at 2.5 or 3.5 is convex in the mean for a low-count process, so a small minutes increase raises the tail probability proportionally more than the mean; the effect is largest for a player whose mean sits near 1.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute P(count >= k) over minutes bins for fixed per-minute rate and compare with Poisson and negative binomial tails.

interactions.hypothesis: A rim protector who contests aggressively both blocks more and fouls more, so the same behaviour that raises block supply raises foul-trouble risk and minute loss; this makes blocks and minutes negatively dependent in the tail.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate correlation between block count and minutes shortfall in games where the player had >=3 first-half fouls.

interactions.hypothesis: A blitz or full-court scheme raises opponent live-ball turnovers only against careless handlers; against a low-turnover primary handler the extra pressure yields deflections without steals, so the effect of scheme on steals is conditional on the opponent handler's turnover rate.
interactions.how_to_test: Interact opponent handler turnover rate with scheme labels in a Poisson regression on team steals.

interactions.hypothesis: Official-scorer credit adds count noise and an arena-specific shift of a few percent of rate (both unverified), which matters most where the count distribution is dense near the threshold: a rate shift of a few percent moves P(3+) for a mean near 1 much more than for a mean near 0.3, so the effect is a mean shift whose impact depends on the distribution shape, not only extra dispersion.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate arena fixed effects on steal and block rates (mean shift) and separately on dispersion over 5 seasons, and check whether the mean shift moves rung hit rates by the amount the shape of the count distribution implies.

interactions.hypothesis: The stocks sum has variance equal to the sum of variances plus twice the covariance; for versatile wings positive covariance raises the 4+ tail relative to independent components, while rim anchors have near-zero covariance.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare P(S+B >= 4) from independent components versus a copula by archetype against realised frequencies.

nonlinearities.shape: convex tail probability in the dispersion parameter
nonlinearities.why: At mean about 1 the probability of 3+ rises from roughly 8% to 12% when the negative-binomial dispersion index moves from 1.0 to 1.4, so rung probability is more sensitive to dispersion than to a 10% change in the mean.

nonlinearities.shape: saturating: shrinkage weight toward the role prior is large
nonlinearities.why: Per-minute rates for steals have a small signal-to-noise ratio across games, so predicted rates should pull strongly toward the role mean; the effective weight on a player's own rate is below 50% for a full season of data.

nonlinearities.shape: threshold at 3-4 fouls triggering benching
nonlinearities.why: For aggressive shot-blockers minutes fall sharply once fouls reach a coach's threshold, so the effect on blocks is a step in minutes rather than a smooth function of the foul rate.

mechanism_review.summary: Steals and blocks are rare counts (typically 0-3 per game) generated by a Poisson-like event process whose rate is the product of minutes, the supply of opportunities and the defender's conversion: steals need live-ball turnovers by opponents and the defender's deflection activity; blocks need opponent rim attempts while the defender is the rim anchor and his contest-to-block conversion. Both are overdispersed because supply varies by opponent style and lineup and because minutes are a mixture, and both carry an additional layer of noise from official-scorer credit decisions. At strikes of 0.5, 1.5 and 2.5 the probability depends more on dispersion and the tail of supply than on the mean, and the stocks contract sums two counts with archetype-specific dependence. The existing catalog uses generic matchup variables; the dominant missing pieces are hustle-based deflections, rim-protector supply, and the sum dependence.

stages.name: Participation and minutes mixture
stages.description: Low-count events scale with court time, so the minutes mixture sets the rate: a blowout cuts the starter's minutes but may raise bench players' attempts to press, and foul trouble affects aggressive defenders. Early exits settle on actual counts because the contract voids only inactive players.
stages.distribution: Mixture over minutes scenarios; the effect on a Poisson rate is multiplicative and dominates at the 2.5 strike.

stages.name: Supply of blockable shots and stealable turnovers
stages.description: Blocks require opponent shots at the rim contested by the player; the supply is the opponent's rim frequency while the player is on court and his share of contests. Steals require live-ball turnovers by opponents, with supply set by the opponent's careless handlers and style. Pace scales both supplies but is second-order to the opponent's shot and turnover mix.
stages.distribution: Supply counts overdispersed relative to Poisson with team-pair dependence (e.g. rim attempts per game vary with sd about 5 around a mean near 28).

stages.name: Defender conversion: deflections, contests and scheme
stages.description: The defender converts opportunities at a stable personal rate: steals per deflection and blocks per contest, modulated by scheme (blitz and zone raise deflections, drop coverage anchors the center near the rim). Rates are persistent but samples are small, so shrinkage towards role priors is needed.
stages.distribution: Thinned Poisson per opportunity with player-specific rates; sampling noise dominates a single-game count.

stages.name: Credit noise and dependence for stocks
stages.description: Official scorers decide steal and block credit, with arena-level tendencies and post-game video review corrections, which adds dispersion at the 0.5/1.5 strike. The stocks contract adds steals and blocks whose dependence differs by archetype: activity-driven for versatile wings, nearly independent for rim anchors.
stages.distribution: Count noise inflated by credit decisions (assumed extra dispersion index of 0.1-0.2 (hypothesis, unverified)); bivariate dependence with archetype-specific correlation 0-0.3.

stages.name: Threshold crossing and settlement
stages.description: The ladder rung is a threshold on an integer count with a small mean, so the probability of 3+ is a tail event highly sensitive to the dispersion assumption: a mean of 0.9 blocks gives 3+ probability of roughly 5% under Poisson and noticeably more with overdispersion. Settlement uses the official box score and refunds only inactive players.
stages.distribution: Tail of a negative binomial with mean 0.5-3; rung probabilities highly convex in the dispersion parameter.

coaching_scheme.note: Pressure and drop schemes change gamble and rim-contest profile.

environment.note: Arena and altitude effects on steals and blocks are negligible beyond the scorer-credit effect handled under officiating; no separate environment variable is justified for these counts.

game_context_script.note: Blowout minutes changes and garbage-time pressing.

pace_volume.note: Opportunity counts scale with possessions but supply is more specific than pace.

efficiency_conversion.note: Conversion of deflections and contests to steals and blocks.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Back-to-back fatigue (lower activity) and minutes ramp-ups after injury affect deflection and contest effort but no input represents them; the size for low-count events is unknown.

contract_review.settlement_definition: Binary ladders on one player's official counts in the named game: blocks at or above N (e.g. 3+ blocks, floor_strike 2.5), steals at or above N (3+ steals) and combined steals plus blocks at or above N (4+, floor 3.5). Inactive players and players who never take the court settle at a fair price; once a player enters, the market settles on his recorded steals/blocks/combination. A postponed game that starts within 48 hours stays open, otherwise all markets resolve at a fair price. No turnover series is present in the ledger despite the archetype name; overtime treatment is not stated in the sampled text.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official box-score steals and blocks as named in the full rules; the sample is truncated before naming source agencies, so the exact source and correction policy are unverified.
variants_and_edge_cases: Strike construction: the sampled rungs are tails for the named players (Shai Gilgeous-Alexander 3+ blocks, Jrue Holiday 3+ steals), i.e. low-probability events in the 3-8% range, so dispersion and credit noise dominate the mean.
Combined stocks (4+, floor 3.5) is a sum of two overdispersed counts; the right-tail probability depends on the covariance and on archetype (a rim protector's stocks are mostly blocks).
Turnovers (the archetype name includes them) have no live series in the ledger, so a turnover contract's rules (assist-to-turnover, team turnovers) are unverified.

Overtime is not mentioned in the sampled rules; if the contract uses the official final box score, steals and blocks would include OT minutes (about five minutes in roughly 6% of games), but this is an assumption: the sampled rules do not say whether overtime counts (sbt-ot-inclusion).

Scope: no turnover series is live, so this record's inputs price steals, blocks and steals-plus-blocks only; any future player-turnover contract would need an own-turnover mechanism that is not defined here.

player_free_throws.label: NBA player free throws made
player_free_throws.target: Player free throws made over a strike
player_free_throws.mechanism: FT made = FT attempts x FT%. Attempts come from foul-drawing skill, shot profile (rim attacks), opponent foul rate, crew calls and late-game fouling script; FT% is a high-signal skill with limited noise at ~80%. Minutes and game script (close game with late fouls) drive the right tail. Blowouts reduce attempts.

Minutes scale attempts for NBA player free throws made.
Crew foul rate shifts attempts.
Opponent foul-committing rate.
Close games produce intentional fouls on ball handlers.
Drives and post touches generate fouls.
Rim attack share predicts FTA.

Blowouts cut late-game FT chances.
Attempt dispersion plus binomial conversion.
