interactions.hypothesis: Team scoring depends on offense/defense interaction in shot profile: rim-heavy offense vs rim-protecting defense differs from generic ratings.
The favorite's team total is shaded down by blowout probability and the underdog's up by late free throws; implied totals from linear spread/total miss this skew.
Own absence of a primary ball handler affects own pace, so both team points and total change.
Team-total, game-total and spread must cohere; incoherence signals a stale market.

Own efficiency against this defense depends on factor-level fit: a rim-heavy offense gains against a drop defense that concedes rim attempts, but loses against one that walls the paint; the additive rating difference averages these opposite cases and so errs systematically for extreme styles.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare error of additive rating prediction versus the four-factor matchup prediction for teams in the top and bottom rim-rate quintiles.

interactions.hypothesis: The favorite's expected points flatten when the game becomes lopsided because starters sit while the underdog's points keep rising through late fouls and bench scoring; the relation of team points to margin is piecewise with a kink around a 10-12 point expected margin.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit a spline of own points on expected margin using ratings and check for the kink separately for favorites and underdogs.

interactions.hypothesis: A missing ball handler lowers both team efficiency and the possession count; the two effects multiply in the points total so a model that adjusts only the rating understates the points drop, and the opponent's points move too through the shared pace.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare team points and possessions in games without the primary handler versus with, controlling for opponent.

interactions.hypothesis: Trailing teams foul late and the leading team shoots the free throws, so crew foul tendency raises the favorite's points more in close games and the underdog's points via fouls drawn in garbage time; effect depends on the margin path.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate FT points by team and margin bin, interacted with crew foul rate.

interactions.hypothesis: A three-point-reliant team has high variance in points, so strikes far from the mean have probability much different from a low-variance team; luck regression (the three-point mean) and variance (the dispersion) are separate parameters that both matter for strike distance.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare calibration of P(over) at strikes 6+ points from the mean using team-specific versus pooled variance.

nonlinearities.shape: threshold with asymmetric effect on favorite and underdog
nonlinearities.why: Beyond about a 15-point margin late, starters sit and the favorite's points fall, while the underdog's points rise slightly; the relation is not monotone in blowout probability and differs by side.

nonlinearities.shape: mixture step: about 6% probability of adding roughly a dozen points if OT counts
nonlinearities.why: The team-points distribution acquires a right-hand lump from OT; the over probability for high strikes is lifted by the mixture while the central probability is nearly unaffected.

nonlinearities.shape: concave in possession count for points: efficiency declines as pace increases
nonlinearities.why: Faster pace raises possessions but lowers per-possession efficiency slightly (quicker shots), so points rise less than proportionally with pace.

mechanism_review.summary: A team's points equal the shared number of possessions times its points per possession, plus overtime if counted. Possessions are a joint property of both teams (the slower style may dominate, a hypothesis to be tested), while points per possession come from the matchup of own offense with the opponent's defense decomposed into shooting, turnovers, offensive rebounds and free throws, with tonight's availability changing every factor. Game script then bends the result: a favorite's points flatten in garbage time, an underdog's rise from late fouling and deep-bench scoring, so team points are a nonlinear function of expected margin. Variance depends on style (three-point reliance, pace) and is large relative to strike spacing, and the settlement wording on overtime determines whether a 6% mixture component of about a dozen points is part of the distribution.

stages.name: Shared possessions
stages.description: The game's possession count is one number determined jointly by both teams' tempo preferences, transition rates and turnovers; averaging the two teams' season paces misstates it, since the slower style may dominate (hypothesis, not established). Lineup changes (a missing point guard) shift tempo for the whole game.
stages.distribution: Roughly normal with mean near 98-100 and sd 4-5 possessions; a right skew from OT; correlated with both teams' scoring.

stages.name: Own offense against the opponent's defense
stages.description: Points per possession depend on own shot quality, turnover and offensive rebound tendencies, free throws and the opponent's defensive profile in each factor. The additive offensive-minus-defensive rating approximates this but the factor decomposition handles scheme-specific deviations such as a rim-heavy offense against a drop defense.
stages.distribution: Efficiency per 100 possessions with sd across teams of about 4; matchup deviations of 1-2 points; per-game noise dominated by three-point variance.

stages.name: Availability and unit changes
stages.description: Absence of own scorers lowers offensive rating and also changes pace; absence of the opponent's rim protector or point-of-attack defender raises it. Starters are confirmed shortly before tip and rotation changes alter the expected minutes of the best units.
stages.distribution: Discrete personnel states with rating shifts of 1-5 points per 100 possessions per key absence.

stages.name: Shooting variance and free throws
stages.description: Single-game three-point shooting luck of both teams, and the foul-and-free-throw environment (crew tendencies, bonus), are the largest random components of points; they regress to expectation between games and have style-dependent variance. Free throws contribute 3-4 points per game across crews.
stages.distribution: Team points sd about 11-14, larger for three-point-reliant teams; shooting shocks are positively correlated between the two teams' totals through pace.

stages.name: Game script and overtime
stages.description: Win probability bends team points: favorites' starters sit in garbage time, underdogs score late through fouling and bench possessions; the mapping from expected margin to team points is nonlinear. Overtime, if counted, adds a mixture component of about a dozen points with probability near 6%.
stages.distribution: Skewed conditional distribution; mixture with an OT component whose size is about 11-13 points and weight about 5-7%.

stages.name: Settlement
stages.description: Settlement is the official final score for the named team above a half-point strike; cancellation and long delays void at a fair price. The sampled rules do not say whether overtime counts, which is the largest unknown.
stages.distribution: Binary indicator on integer points; no push.

contract_review.settlement_definition: KXNBATEAMTOTAL is a binary over/under on one named team's points in the named game: YES if the team scores more than the half-point strike (floor_strike 135.5, strike_type greater, so no push). A game postponed but starting within 48 hours stays open and resolves on the official final result; a game cancelled or not started within 48 hours resolves all markets at a fair price. The sampled rules do not say whether overtime points count, so the OT inclusion that the existing draft asserts is not verified; the ledger has only one series for this archetype.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official final score of the game as published by the league; the sampled rules refer to 'the official final result' without naming a provider.
variants_and_edge_cases: Overtime: the sampled primary and secondary text never mention overtime; 'the official final result' of a game normally includes OT points, which would add roughly 11-13 points to each team in about 6% of games, but this is unverified and changes tail probabilities.

Strike construction: the sampled strike of 135.5 for Oklahoma City is well above a typical team total (about 115-120), consistent with a ladder of rungs; the contract is a single threshold per market with no push at half-point strikes.

Team total is not a function of a single team's offense: it depends on the shared possession count and the opponent's play, so correlated markets (game total, spread, opponent team total) must be internally consistent.
Void on cancellation or a delay beyond 48 hours pays a fair price, so late-season games affected by weather or travel have no NO risk but no information either.

quarter_and_half_markets.mechanism: Period scoring depends on lineups on the floor in that period (starters in Q1 and Q3, bench-heavy stretches in Q2 and Q4), period pace, and game state. Q1 is the most pregame-predictable (starters known), Q4 depends on score state and fouling. Period totals have wide relative variance, tie probability matters for winners, and the sum of period lines should reconcile with the game total.

2H totals and margins depend on when starters sit, which depends on first-half margin and coach policy.
Opening-quarter pace differs from game pace and is team-specific; combine both teams' Q1 pace tendencies.
Periods exclude OT unless stated; a mismatch with game-level markets creates edges when books price with OT.

Team Q1 history is valid only if tonight's starting five matches the historical one; a changed starter makes the stored Q1 rating stale, and the loss is larger for first and third quarters than for second and fourth, where the bench pattern matters more.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare Q1 margin prediction error when the starting five is the modal five versus when one starter differs, holding team rating fixed.

interactions.hypothesis: Second-half lineups depend on the first-half margin: when the margin exceeds roughly 15 at halftime coaches shorten Q3 starter minutes and use bench units in Q4, so Q3 and Q4 are two different regimes whose scoring rates differ in both pace and efficiency.

interactions.hypothesis: Because 2H contracts include overtime and Q4 contracts do not, the 2H total is Q3 plus Q4 plus an overtime component with probability about 5-7% and size about 22-26 combined points (about 11-13 per team), producing a right-skew in the 2H total and a wedge to Q3+Q4 prices.
interactions.how_to_test: Decompose 2H total into regulation and OT parts in history and compare tail probabilities of the 2H total with and without the OT mixture component.

interactions.hypothesis: Tie probability and margin variance both rise as possessions per period fall because fewer scoring events produce smaller margins; slow-pace matchups therefore have higher tie mass and lower probability of crossing 7.5/8.5 margin strikes.
interactions.how_to_test: Bin quarters by projected possessions and compare empirical tie frequency and exceedance rates at 7.5.

interactions.hypothesis: End-of-quarter fouling when the team is in the bonus produces clusters of free throws at near-100% value; this convexly raises Q4 totals when the game is within 5 points, whereas early-quarter fouls matter less because bonus onset is later.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare Q4 FTA and points per possession in the final two minutes by margin bin and team-foul count.

nonlinearities.shape: discrete, peaked at zero with excess kurtosis (Skellam-like)
nonlinearities.why: Winner, tie and spread-at-7.5 contracts cut a discrete integer distribution at specific points; a Gaussian approximation misstates tie mass and tail probability by 1-2 percentage points.

nonlinearities.shape: threshold: Q4 regime switch when margin exceeds about 15-18 entering Q4
nonlinearities.why: Starters are removed once the game is decided so Q4 pace and efficiency change discontinuously; effect on Q4 total and margin is small until the threshold.

nonlinearities.shape: step: effect of a missing starter on Q1 is larger than a proportional rating drop
nonlinearities.why: A missing starter changes all four teammates' lineup context in Q1 and also removes the scripted first-stint plays; the rating loss of the unit exceeds the player's marginal contribution.

nonlinearities.shape: concave: possessions saturate in fast periods while slow periods cluster tightly
nonlinearities.why: Pace is bounded by the 24-second clock so possession counts have limited upside but can drop sharply in lopsided Q4s.

mechanism_review.summary: A quarter or half is a short scoring contest of roughly 24 possessions per team whose outcome is determined by who is on the floor in that segment, the number of possessions, efficiency per possession and small-sample noise, with score-state feedback across periods. The chain is: starters and rotation templates by quarter (Q1 and Q3 starters, Q2 bench-heavy, Q4 closers or garbage time), the period possession count (fast starts, slow lopsided Q4), unit-level offensive and defensive strength against the opponent's units, shooting variance that is large relative to a 24-possession sample, foul and bonus timing that resets each quarter, end-of-period shot-clock possessions, and the settlement rule (overtime excluded from quarters and first half, included in the second half for KXNBA2H, KXNBA2HSPREAD and KXNBA2HTOTAL but excluded for KXNBA2HWINNER; ties pay a separate market). Because the sample is small, period margin is a noisy integer variable whose discreteness (ties, half-point cut points) matters, and most information comes from lineup identity and rotation structure rather than team-season averages.

stages.name: Lineups and rotation templates by quarter
stages.description: Coaches deploy starters for the first six to eight minutes, stagger substitutions into Q2, restart with starters in Q3 and then use closers or reserves in Q4 depending on score. Which five play in each period, and who is absent, determine the strength of the units. Starters confirmed shortly before tip are the most valuable late information for Q1 and Q3 markets; Q2 and Q4 depend on bench availability and coaching style.
stages.distribution: Discrete personnel states by quarter; the Q1 state is nearly deterministic after the starters are announced while Q4 is a mixture dependent on score.

stages.name: Period possessions and pace
stages.description: Possessions per period reflect both teams' tendencies and game state: fast early periods, decreased pace in lopsided late periods, long possessions at the end of a quarter. Period pace is not the game pace; each team's style and the identity of the units determine it, and totals markets scale with this count.
stages.distribution: Approximately normal around 24-26 possessions per team with sd about 2.5; correlated across the two teams and right-skewed by end-of-period shot-clock dynamics.

stages.name: Unit efficiency and matchup
stages.description: Each unit's points per possession against the opponent's units come from ratings of the relevant players, shot profile and defensive scheme. Opponent-adjusted ratings from full games blur unit differences, especially in Q2 and Q4, where bench-heavy units dominate. Matchup-specific mismatches (a bench big against a switching unit) matter more in short periods.
stages.distribution: Unit PPP roughly normal across units (sd of unit ratings about 6 per 100 possessions) with large sampling noise per period.

stages.name: Small-sample scoring noise and the margin distribution
stages.description: With about 24 possessions per team the sd of a team's quarter points is around five and the margin sd around seven; shooting luck therefore dominates and the probability mass at small integer margins (including the tie) cannot be treated as continuous. Hot starts regress rather than carry into later periods, so period luck is nearly independent across quarters.
stages.distribution: Discrete difference of two near-Poisson-binomial scores (Skellam-like) with excess kurtosis; tie mass of about 4-6% per quarter, higher in low-pace periods.

stages.name: Score-state feedback, halftime adjustments and foul resets
stages.description: Leads and trailing affect later periods: leading teams in the 2H may rest starters early, Q3 sees halftime adjustments, Q4 sees intentional fouling and clock management. Team fouls reset each quarter so bonus free throws cluster late in periods; end-of-quarter possessions and heaves shift totals. These effects are small for Q1 but central for Q4 and 2H markets.
stages.distribution: State-dependent mixture: Q4 and 2H are regime-switching with blowout versus close-game regimes; foul effects add right-skew to period totals.

stages.name: Settlement partitions and cross-market identities
stages.description: The contracts partition the game: Q1+Q2=1H and Q3+Q4 = regulation second half, to which overtime is added only for KXNBA2H, KXNBA2HSPREAD and KXNBA2HTOTAL; KXNBA2HWINNER and all quarter series stop at regulation. A game tied after regulation triggers a five-minute overtime that adds roughly 22-26 combined points (about 11-13 per team) to the OT-inclusive 2H series only. Period winners carry a tie outcome. Consistency across period totals and the game total is an identity, not a signal, and the series-specific rule text defines which points count.
stages.distribution: Deterministic sum identities with a mixture over OT presence; P(OT) roughly 5-7% overall, taken from the zero mass of the ratings-implied regulation margin rather than a spread bucket, plus a small multi-OT tail.

stages.name: In-play conditioning for later-period markets
stages.description: Because the second-half and later-quarter markets stay open until a winner is declared, a quote placed during the game is a bet on the remaining part of a period given what has already happened. The value is the conditional distribution of the remaining margin given the current score, period start score, clock, the lineups actually on the floor, team-foul and bonus state and timeouts. Pregame inputs set the prior; the live state dominates once a period is under way.
stages.distribution: Remaining-margin variance shrinks roughly linearly with remaining possessions; a period lead late in the quarter makes the outcome near-deterministic, with discrete jumps at each score.

contract_review.settlement_definition: Period contracts settle on points scored in a defined segment of the named game: quarter and half winner (the team scoring more points in the period), 'tie' contracts (YES if neither team wins the period), spreads (named team wins the period by more than X.5), totals (combined period points above X.5) and team totals (one team's period points above X.5). Quarters 1-4 and the first half count regulation points only. The second half differs by family: KXNBA2H, KXNBA2HSPREAD and KXNBA2HTOTAL say '(including overtime)', while KXNBA2HWINNER covers 'the second half (excluding overtime)'. Two winner families coexist: KXNBA1Q-4Q/KXNBA1H/KXNBA2H list a separate tie contract, and the KXNBA*WINNER series state that on equal points all team strikes resolve No and the Tie strike Yes; the WINNER family keeps postponed games open until the rescheduled game ends within two weeks, while the spread/total/tie texts sampled show no postponement wording. KXNBA1QTEAMTOTAL and KXNBA4QTEAMTOTAL are TITLE_ONLY.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official game linescore / play-by-play scoring by period from the named league sources; the sampled period rules do not name the source agencies.
variants_and_edge_cases: Overtime inclusion differs by series, not only by period: Q1-Q4 and 1H exclude OT; KXNBA2H, KXNBA2HSPREAD and KXNBA2HTOTAL include it; KXNBA2HWINNER excludes it. A game tied after regulation adds roughly 22-26 combined points to 2H totals and spreads but cannot change the KXNBA2HWINNER result.

Winner contracts are three-way: the KXNBA1Q-4Q/1H/2H series list 'tie' as its own contract and the WINNER family pays a Tie strike while team strikes resolve No, so a model must output a three-way probability with integer tie mass.

Sampled strikes are far from central values (1st quarter total 71.5, 2nd quarter total 70.5, 2nd half total 135.5) and 1H team total 64.5, consistent with ladders of rungs; which rungs are live is not stated in the rules.
Spread strikes are half-points (7.5, 8.5), so no push exists; a tied period is NO for any team-wins-by-X spread.
Postponement: the WINNER family stays open until a rescheduled game finishes within two weeks; the sampled tie/spread/total texts carry no postponement sentence, so their void handling is not read.

The WINNER-family samples (KXNBA1QWINNER-KXNBA4QWINNER, KXNBA1HWINNER, KXNBA2HWINNER) are finalized markets from the 26JUN13 New York vs San Antonio Finals game, while the tie/spread/total samples are November 2026 regular-season markets; whether the WINNER family is still listed with the same wording is not verified.

game_overtime_and_team_events.mechanism: Overtime requires a regulation tie: probability follows the margin density at zero (about 5-6% unconditional), higher in tight spreads and slightly higher for slower games, and independent of spread outside narrow ranges. Bench-points markets scale with starter minutes, bench quality and blowout probability; the definition of bench (non-starters) interacts with lineup changes. Team-stat head-to-heads compare two correlated counts where pace correlation shrinks variance.

interactions.hypothesis: P(OT) is about the margin pmf at zero which is flat across typical spreads; do not over-model it by team.
Bench points rise with blowout probability only when the bench is scoring-capable; correlate with margin.
A rested starter becomes a bench player in the market's definition, mechanically raising bench points if the scorer plays.
Wording for multiple OT periods and for 'game goes to overtime' vs 'tie after regulation' is part of the target definition.

The tie probability is the Gaussian pmf at zero, which decays like exp(-mu^2/(2 sigma^2)); the loss from a 4-point expected margin to a 10-point expected margin is far larger than from 0 to 4, so the effect of expected margin on P(OT) is convex-then-flat in the tail.
interactions.how_to_test: Bin games by own-model expected margin (0-2, 2-5, 5-8, 8-12, 12+) and compare the observed OT rate with the Gaussian prediction and with a flat rate.

interactions.hypothesis: The excess tie mass is conditional on the game being within three points with under 30 seconds left and on the trailing coach's policy; if the leading team intentionally fouls, ties become less likely than by smooth density.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate P(tie | within 3 at 0:30) by coach pair and contrast with fouling versus non-fouling policies.

interactions.hypothesis: When the top scorer is promoted into the starting five by an absence, he leaves the bench count and bench points drop by his share; when a returning star plays off the bench on a restriction, bench points rise by his minutes times his rate, a discrete jump.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare bench points in games with promoted-starter and with star-off-bench changes versus baselines.

interactions.hypothesis: Bench minutes rise with blowout probability but saturate once starters sit entirely, around 150-170 minutes; beyond that extra blowout size adds nothing, while within the competitive range additional margin adds quickly.
interactions.how_to_test: Plot bench minutes against final margin to find the saturation; fit a piecewise-linear spline.

interactions.hypothesis: The two teams' counts rise and fall together with pace, so a pace shock moves both and leaves the difference nearly unchanged; the difference's sd is smaller than independent counts would give, and the covariance is higher in games with competitive scores.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate rho of team threes by pace tercile and by closeness of final score.

interactions.hypothesis: The trailing team raises its three-point attempt share late in lopsided games while the leader slows down, so the expected made-threes difference shrinks toward zero (or flips) in blowout scripts even when the favourite is the higher-volume team; this cuts the favourite's edge in KXNBAH2HTEAM3PT.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress the fourth-quarter team 3PA share difference on the projected margin bucket and compare the H2H threes outcome rate by margin bucket against the volume-only prediction.

nonlinearities.shape: Gaussian bell in the expected margin with an empirical multiplicative excess
nonlinearities.why: P(OT) falls as exp(-(expected margin/sigma)^2/2), so it declines by about 30% at a 10-point expected margin, and the excess factor lifts all levels by about 1.7-1.9.

nonlinearities.shape: Piecewise: flat in close games, rising then saturating in blowouts
nonlinearities.why: Bench minutes are about 90-100 when close, grow rapidly when margin exceeds 15, and cap near the whole-bench total once starters sit.

nonlinearities.shape: Geometric decay in number of OT periods
nonlinearities.why: Each extra overtime period occurs with a small probability that is roughly constant, so tail periods add little mass and multi-OT strike markets are rare events with unstable estimates.

nonlinearities.shape: convex tail in per-game tie probability and dispersion
nonlinearities.why: P(3+ OT games in a series) scales roughly with the cube of the per-game OT rate and rises sharply with within-series dependence, so a 20% error in the per-game rate becomes roughly a 70% error in the 3+ tail.

mechanism_review.summary: Overtime is the event that regulation margin equals zero, so its probability is the probability mass of the end-of-regulation margin distribution at a single integer. With margin approximately normal with mean mu (the own-model expected margin, not the closing spread) and sd sigma near 12, that mass is phi(mu/sigma)/sigma, about 3.3% at a pick-em, falling to about 2.3% at a 10-point expected margin and about 1.7% at 14; the observed overall rate is higher, near 6%, because end-of-game strategy (tie-seeking threes, intentional fouling and clock management) piles extra probability at zero and small margins. So P(OT) is strongly decreasing in |spread|, not flat, and is higher for slow, low-variance games. Bench-points markets are different: the outcome is the sum of points from non-starters, a function of how many minutes the bench plays (240 minus starter minutes, plus 25 in OT), the bench's points per minute, and the official starter list that defines who counts. Team-stat head-to-heads compare two correlated counts (the pace shared by both teams creates positive correlation), so the sign and size of the difference depend on volumes and rates, not on a margin tie mass.

stages.name: Regulation margin density at zero
stages.description: P(OT) equals the probability that the regulation margin lands on 0. With the mean set by availability-adjusted ratings and the sd set by pace and the favourite's size, the Gaussian body gives the baseline mass at zero, and that mass shrinks roughly like exp(-mu^2 / (2 sigma^2)); a 12-point favourite is about 40% less likely to need overtime than a pick-em. Slow, low-total games have smaller sigma and so slightly more mass at zero.
stages.distribution: Single-integer mass of a near-normal density, about 3.3% at a pick-em from the Gaussian alone; heteroscedastic in pace; empirical excess to about 6% overall from late-game structure.

stages.name: Late-game tie-forcing strategy
stages.description: In the last minute, the trailing team down by three can attempt a tying three, the leading team can foul to prevent it or defend the three, and clock management determines possessions left. Intentional fouling turns near-ties into free-throw sequences whose outcomes concentrate at margins of 1-4 points. This end-of-game structure puts probability exactly on zero that a smooth margin model misses, and the amount depends on coach policy, free-throw shooting of the ball handlers and whether the team leads by 3.
stages.distribution: Excess point mass at 0 and at +/-1 to 3 compared to a Gaussian; amount is policy-dependent and not captured by ratings.

stages.name: Overtime length and what it adds
stages.description: Given overtime, the game adds one five-minute period (about 22-26 total points) with a second OT in a minority of overtime games, adding starter-heavy minutes to both teams, which changes the starter/bench split and the team stat counts for the head-to-heads if 'full game' includes OT. KXNBASERIESOT asks for at least N overtime games (3+ in the Finals sample) across a best-of-seven: the count is a Poisson-binomial over a random number of games (4 to 7) with per-game tie probabilities from each game's own-model margin, inflated by positive within-series correlation of closeness; at p near 6% the 3+ event sits deep in the tail, so the dispersion parameter and the series-length distribution matter more than the mean OT rate.
stages.distribution: OT periods: geometric-like with P(second OT | first OT) about 0.07-0.10; series OT-game count: overdispersed Poisson-binomial mixture over series length, P(>=3) of order 1%.

stages.name: Bench minutes and bench scoring rate
stages.description: Bench points = bench minutes times bench points per minute. Bench minutes are what is left after the starters' minutes, which fall in blowouts and when foul trouble hits, and rise when a starter is out and the bench is deep. The points per minute reflect bench scorers' usage, which depends on whether a sixth man is a primary scorer and on the second unit's lineup. The definition of bench via the starter list moves the target when a starter is rested.
stages.distribution: Bench points have sd about 8 around means of about 35 points; strongly state-dependent (blowout state shifts bench minutes by 20+). Non-negative, right-skewed.

stages.name: Team-stat pair distribution
stages.description: KXNBAH2HTEAM3PT compares team A and team B made threes; each count is team three-point attempts (team 3PA rate per possession against the opponent's 3PA allowed, times shared possessions) times a make rate regressed toward shot quality. The counts are positively correlated through shared pace and negatively through score state (the trailing team takes more threes late), so the difference is narrower than independent counts. The 50/50 tie rule means the 7-9% exact-tie mass is split, and overtime adds attempts to both sides.
stages.distribution: Difference of two overdispersed counts with correlation about +0.2 to 0.3 from shared pace; discrete with a mass at zero.

contract_review.settlement_definition: Five live series, all with recovered rules text. KXNBAOT: Yes if at least 1 overtime period is played in the named game (48-hour postponement rule, fair price if cancelled or not started within 48 hours). KXNBAOVERTIME: Yes if the two teams 'go to overtime' in the named game (same event; no postponement clause in its text). KXNBASERIESOT: Yes if at least N games (sampled: 3+) go to overtime in a named playoff series (sampled: the Finals), i.e. a count threshold over a random-length series, not a single indicator. KXNBAH2HBENCHPTS and KXNBAH2HTEAM3PT: Yes if team A records more total bench points / more made three-pointers than team B 'in the full game'; an exact tie resolves 50/50; a game cancelled or postponed more than two weeks resolves to a fair market price. Not stated: whether 'full game' includes overtime (likely, not explicit), the definition of 'bench' (official non-starters), and stat-correction handling (u1, u4).
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official box score / play-by-play: period count for overtime, official starters for the bench split, team made threes; the rules name no source explicitly.
variants_and_edge_cases: Single-game overtime (KXNBAOT, KXNBAOVERTIME) is an indicator of regulation ending tied; multiple overtimes do not change the result.

Series overtime (KXNBASERIESOT) is a count threshold ('at least 3 games' in the sampled Finals market): with per-game P(OT) near 6%, P(>=3 of 4-7 games) is a rare tail event (order 1%) dominated by series length and within-series closeness correlation; other thresholds (1+, 2+) may be listed.

Head-to-head ties resolve 50/50 (both bench points and team threes); for team threes (means about 12-15 per team) the exact-tie mass is about 7-9%, for bench points (sd of the difference near 11) about 3-4%.
'Full game' is not defined: overtime most likely counts, adding roughly 5 minutes of starter-heavy play (bench share low), which matters for bench points more than for threes (u1).
Bench definition: bench points are points by players who did not start; a late starter change promotes a reserve out of the bench count. The rules do not name the source for starter designation (u4).
Postponement windows differ inside the archetype: 48 hours for KXNBAOT, two weeks for the head-to-heads, unstated for KXNBAOVERTIME and KXNBASERIESOT.

race_to_and_points_leader.label: NBA race-to-N and game points leader
race_to_and_points_leader.target: Which team reaches N points first; which player scores the most points in the game
race_to_and_points_leader.mechanism: Race-to-N is a first-passage problem on two scoring processes driven by early-game pace, efficiency and starters; ties of rate make home-court and first possession matter. Points leader selects the maximum of several players' point distributions across both teams: it depends on minutes, usage, efficiency, overtime, and blowout minutes loss, with ties handled per rules. Both are sensitive to the starting five.

inputs.why: Early lineups determine both processes.

First-possession advantage is worth little for N=20+ but matters for N=5-10.

Race thresholds below 15 depend almost entirely on the identity of the starters and the opening tempo; a starter swap changes the scoring-event mix per possession, and the effect is largest when the replaced player is the primary creator.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare first-passage times to 10 points by starter-change indicator, controlling for opponent and opening possession.

interactions.hypothesis: First possession is hypothesised to be worth about half a possession in points (unverified); in a race to 5-10 it is a large share of the total edge but for N of 25 or above it is swamped by rating gap and noise, so the effect shrinks like 1/sqrt(N).
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate the opening-possession coefficient separately for each N in the logistic race model and check the decline.

interactions.hypothesis: When a co-star sits the top scorer's expected points rise and a rival for the leader title disappears, so the leader probability grows faster than the usage gain alone; the effect on the opposing team's best scorer is the opposite.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare leader share of a star in games with and without his top teammate, holding opponent and minutes.

interactions.hypothesis: Overtime favors the highest-minutes stars while blowouts remove the favorite's stars; leader probability therefore switches between a star-dominated regime in close games and a bench-diluted regime in lopsided ones.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate leader share by star team win-probability bin and OT indicator.

interactions.hypothesis: Negative same-team correlation in points lowers the chance of both teammates scoring high, so the maximum is often a single outlier; positive cross-team correlation via pace increases both sides' high tails, spreading leader probability across teams.
interactions.how_to_test: Simulate max with the observed covariance vs independent marginals and compare to realised leader frequencies.

nonlinearities.shape: convex/softmax-like: leader probability rises faster than expected points gap
nonlinearities.why: The maximum of several heavy-tailed variables gives winner-take-all behavior; a player with a modest expected-points edge over the second option wins disproportionately more often because the field is split among many low-probability candidates.

nonlinearities.shape: decaying like 1/sqrt(N) in the race threshold
nonlinearities.why: First-possession advantage is a roughly constant half possession of points while the standard deviation of the margin at N points grows with N, so the probability edge declines with N.

nonlinearities.shape: piecewise with an OT step and blowout truncation
nonlinearities.why: Stars' minutes jump by about five in OT games and are cut in lopsided games, making leader probability a discontinuous function of projected game closeness.

mechanism_review.summary: Race-to-N is a first-passage problem on two alternating-possession scoring processes with lumpy 0-3 point outcomes, so the winner is determined by who starts with the ball, the starters' first-stint scoring rates and the early-game noise, with the first-possession edge hypothesised at roughly half a possession (unverified) and diminishing relative to noise as N grows. Points leader is the argmax over around twenty players' final points, driven by minutes (including overtime and blowout cuts), usage allocation within the unit, per-shot efficiency and a heavy-tailed scoring distribution, with negative dependence between teammates and positive dependence across teams through pace. Both contracts are winner-take-all functionals of the underlying scoring processes, so the tails and dependence matter far more than means, and settlement details (ties, overtime) change the answer materially.

stages.name: Opening conditions: tip, starters and first possession
stages.description: The race starts with the opening tip determining first possession and with the identity of the starters, confirmed only shortly before tip. The first possession is hypothesised to be worth about half a possession (unverified, to be estimated from play-by-play) in expected points, which is a large share of the total edge for small N and a minor one for N of 25 or more. Starter changes shift early scoring rates immediately.
stages.distribution: Binary tip outcome near 50/50 with weak team dependence; starters a discrete state known late; early scoring edge is assumed to scale as the inverse of sqrt(N) (to be tested).

stages.name: Alternating-possession scoring dynamics
stages.description: Each possession ends in 0, 1, 2 or 3 points (with and-ones and free throws as lumps) and possession passes to the other team after a made field goal. The time to N points is a sum of lumpy renewals with correlation between teams induced by alternation, and per-possession efficiency of the starters against the opposing starters determines the winner.
stages.distribution: First-passage of two correlated renewal-reward processes with increments in {0,1,2,3}; overshoot and lumpiness matter at small N; the lead changes frequently.

stages.name: Participation and minutes of candidate leaders
stages.description: For the leader contract, each candidate's minutes are a mixture: full starter load, blowout trimming, foul trouble, early exit and overtime. The pool of plausible leaders shrinks to the top two to three scorers per team, so the minutes tail of those stars largely determines the winner.
stages.distribution: Mixture with left-tail and OT bump; the minutes of the top scorers are positively correlated with a close game.

stages.name: Shot allocation, efficiency and the tail of points
stages.description: Given minutes, a candidate's points depend on usage within the unit and shooting efficiency. Teammate absences concentrate scoring on fewer players and remove competitors for the title. Points distributions have a heavy right tail, so the maximum is often set by an outlier shooting night.
stages.distribution: Right-skewed, overdispersed points per player; negatively correlated within team given team total, positively across teams.

stages.name: Selection of the maximum and settlement
stages.description: The leader is the argmax over the candidate set; leader probability depends on the gap in expected points to the nearest rival and on the variance of each, and decays quickly with the gap. Settlement is read from the rules: co-leaders split $1/N, so near-equal stars carry partial payouts; inactive players score 0 and settle NO, so P(active) multiplies the whole price; the race is won by the team whose score first reaches N.
stages.distribution: Winner-take-all functional (max of correlated heavy-tailed variables); probability concentrated in top few candidates; ties possible at integer maxima.

talent_strength.note: Starter-first-stint strength for the race and scoring ability of the top candidates for the leader market.

opponent_matchup.note: Opposing starters' defense in the first stint and rim protection facing the candidates.

role_personnel.note: Which five start and how scoring is allocated and correlated among the stars.

availability_news.note: Star availability changes the leader candidate set; vintage matters.

coaching_scheme.note: Opening play-calling (set plays for the first possession, early timeouts) and substitution timing of stars within the first stint are coach-specific, but no input in this archetype captures them.

environment.note: Neither contract has a venue-specific mechanism beyond what pace and starters already encode; home court has a small effect on early scoring and is absorbed in the race regression covariate.

game_context_script.note: Blowout trimming and OT affect leader; opening possession affects race.

pace_volume.note: Early-game possession rate for the race; full-game pace for the leader.

efficiency_conversion.note: Starters' per-possession scoring and candidates' scoring efficiency.

distribution_variance.note: First-passage distribution, argmax distribution and dependence structure.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Rest and motivation operate through starter availability and minutes, which are already represented; neither contract has a separate rest or stakes mechanism worth a standalone variable.

officiating_rules.note: Foul-call tendency affects early free-throw runs and star minutes, but no officiating input is attached; whether crew assignment is informative for first-to-N is unmeasured.

settlement_contract.note: Leader ties pay 1/N, inactive players count as 0 points (no void), race is team-based single-game; overtime inclusion for the leader is implied by 'end of the game' but not explicit.

contract_review.settlement_definition: Two live series, both with sampled rules. KXNBARACE is a single-game TEAM race: YES if the named team is 'the first to score' N points in the named game (sample: New Orleans reaches 30 first vs Golden State). KXNBAPTSLEADER is a single-game argmax over all players of both teams: YES if the named player records the most points in the game; co-leaders split, with Yes paying $1/N (rounded down) for N tied players; a player who is inactive or never enters is deemed to have scored 0 points, so he settles NO rather than void. For both, a game postponed but starting within 48 hours stays open and resolves on the official final result, otherwise all markets resolve to a fair price. Neither text says whether overtime points count for the leader (overtime is part of the official final result in normal usage) nor what happens if neither team reaches N.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official final result and box score of the named game (the sampled rules say 'resolve based on the official final result' for postponed games); play-by-play scoring order is needed to determine who reached N first. The specific source agencies are not named in the sample.
variants_and_edge_cases: Leader ties pay $1/N: for two near-equal stars the payout is a mixture of 1, 1/2 and 0, so the tied-maximum probability (to be computed from box scores, plausibly several percent of games) must be modelled, not ignored.

Inactive equals 0 points for the leader contract: a questionable star's price is P(plays) x P(leads | plays), so the injury-status vintage enters at full weight, unlike points ladders where inactive players are voided.

Race to N is team-based and single-game; the sample has N = 30, a level usually reached late in the first quarter or early in the second, so the opening possession matters little and first-stint unit strength and pace dominate. Other N values may be listed; the rules do not fix a set.
Neither team reaching N is possible only for large N or an abandoned game; the race text gives no NO/void rule for it, and for N = 30 it is practically impossible in a completed game.
Overtime: the leader rules say 'at the end of the game' and resolve on the official final result, which suggests OT points count, but the text does not say so explicitly (open item rl-no-rules).

first_basket.label: NBA first basket scorer / first team to score
first_basket.target: Which player scores the first basket (or team scores first) of the game
first_basket.mechanism: P(player scores first) = P(team scores first) x P(player is the scorer | team's first basket). Tip and opening-set plays determine possession; first-shot allocation is designed (ATO/opening play) and concentrated in the starters; make probability on the first shot is near league average. Conditional on starters it is mainly a usage and set-play problem with small samples. Player must start; rules cover postponement and tip ordering.

Without it the stale share of an injured starter's replacement is applied to a new combination.

interactions.hypothesis: Player history is conditional on lineup; a new starter changes everything.
A big who wins the tip but is a low-usage player contributes to team-first but not to player-first.
Opening plays aimed at rim or corner three give higher first-shot make probability than average.

Winning the tip raises the team's first-score probability only by the chain factor, and the gain shrinks when the opponent's opening conversion is high because the loser gets the next possession quickly; the effect is conditional on the opponent's pB.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare P(team scores first | wins tip) versus pB bucket on historical games; expect gap narrowing as pB rises.

interactions.hypothesis: A newly promoted starter inherits the scripted plays of the old slot only partially; the probability that he takes the first shot is conditional on the slot and on the game-count of the new five.
interactions.how_to_test: Contrast first-shot share for replacement starters in their first 5 games versus after 15 games.

interactions.hypothesis: Make probability of the opening shot is shot-type base rate times the opponent's allowed rate in that zone; a rim opener against a drop coverage that concedes mid-range is lower than the base rim rate.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress first-attempt makes on type, opponent zone allowance and their interaction using 3 seasons of openers.

interactions.hypothesis: When one starter is out, scripted shots reallocate to the remaining one or two creators and the first-basket probabilities of the five are negatively correlated, so a single player's share cannot rise without reducing others.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit the share model as a Dirichlet over the five and test whether adding an absent-starter dummy shifts mass to the usage leader.

nonlinearities.shape: Saturating in pA, convex in the product (1-pA)(1-pB)
nonlinearities.why: The race formula flattens as pA approaches the opponent's pB, so equal teams stay near 0.5 and team-first sits near 0.5 + (2q-1)/6 for equal conversion (q the tip-win probability), so a 55-60% jumper moves it by only about 1.7-3.3 points and only large conversion gaps move it further.

nonlinearities.shape: Convex: stars take a disproportionate first-shot share
nonlinearities.why: Observed first-shot share rises faster than usage for the lead scorer because plays are called for the star, so linear usage proportions understate star probabilities and overstate role players'.

nonlinearities.shape: Threshold near about 10-15 games
nonlinearities.why: The scripted share converges to the stable pattern after a few weeks together; weight on history changes sharply for a new five and then flattens.

mechanism_review.summary: Scope note: no live series is filed under this key after the reconciliation (the overtime series formerly misfiled here moved to game_overtime_and_team_events), so everything below is conditional on a first-basket or first-team-to-score series being listed. The first basket is a race between two teams over the first few possessions followed by a draw of one scorer from that team's initial shooters. The chain is: who controls the tip (a near coin flip decided by the two centres' jump-ball ability and the officials' toss), whether the possessing team scores before the other (a geometric race in which each possession converts with probability near the opening-possession points per possession), which player takes the first shot (opening sets are scripted for the starters, so allocation follows the starting five, the coach's opening plays and the first-six-minute usage, not season usage), and whether that shot type converts (a rim or corner three has a different make rate from a pull-up). The outcome is categorical with ten main outcomes plus a thin tail for substitutes, each with probability usually 4-18%, so it is a small-probability, high-variance event where information is concentrated in the starting five confirmation about 30 minutes before tip and in scripted-play evidence. Season-long first-basket counts are tiny samples and unreliable on their own.

stages.name: Starting five and eligibility
stages.description: Only players on court at the tip, plus the rare substitute who enters before the first made basket, can score first; the starting five is announced about 30 minutes before tip, so markets that close earlier carry a mixture over lineups. A late scratch of a starter promotes a bench player into the opening set, redistributing first-shot share to different players and slots. Confirmation timing and the identity of the replacement starter determine the choice set.
stages.distribution: Categorical with a rare substitution branch; lineup uncertainty before confirmation is a discrete mixture over 2-3 candidate starting fives with probabilities updated at the injury report and at confirmation.

stages.name: Tip control and possession order
stages.description: The jump ball between the two starting centres decides who has the first possession; ability is about height and reach with some teams choosing a guard to jump. The advantage for a better jumper is modest, around a 55-60% win rate for a strong jumper against an average one. Winning the tip is not the same as scoring first because the other side gets the next possession when the first one fails. Because the tip winner holds the first possession, the team-first probability is q * pA/(1-(1-pA)(1-pB)) + (1-q) * (1 - pB/(1-(1-pA)(1-pB))) with q the tip-win probability, so a 55% jumper moves team-first by only about 1.7 points and a 60% jumper by about 3.3 points at pA = pB = 0.5.
stages.distribution: Bernoulli with probability near 0.5, shifted by jumper matchup; with equal conversion the downstream effect on P(team scores first) is (2q-1)/6, about 1.7 points for a 55% jumper and 3.3 points for a 60% jumper.

stages.name: First-possession race
stages.description: Given possession, team A scores on its first trip with probability pA (opening possession points per possession close to the team's early-quarter efficiency), else B gets the ball and scores with pB, alternating. P(A scores first | A has the ball) = pA / (1 - (1-pA)(1-pB)), which is about 0.67 when pA = pB = 0.5 (0.5/0.75) and about 0.64 at pA = 0.45, pB = 0.5, so the team with the first possession scores first about two times in three, i.e. about 33 points more often than the team without it (17 points above an even 0.5). Pace matters little because the race ends within about three trips, but turnovers, early fouls and offensive rebounds extend it. The trip is the unit, and a trip can end in a made field goal, a foul with free throws, a turnover or a miss with a rebound; whether pA counts only made field goals or any first scoring event depends on the unresolved free-throw rule.
stages.distribution: Truncated geometric race, near 0.5 for each team; rapidly converging so variance is almost entirely from the first two possessions.

stages.name: Opening set and first-shot allocation
stages.description: Coaches script the opening plays for specific players (a post touch for the centre, a pick-and-roll for the guard), so the share of first shots by player depends on the starting five, the opponent's defensive alignment and the coach's habits, and is not equal to season usage. Usage over the first six minutes of games measures it far better than season usage, and new starting fives reset the pattern. Teammate absence concentrates the first shot in the remaining stars.
stages.distribution: Categorical over the five starters with Dirichlet-like uncertainty; per-player first-shot share has a small effective sample (about 70 first possessions per season per team), which demands hierarchical shrinkage to early-game usage.

stages.name: First-shot conversion and the follow-up
stages.description: The first shot's make rate depends on type: layups and dunks convert near 60-65%, corner threes near 38%, pull-ups lower; misses lead to rebounds and a second attempt by often a different player (a putback by a big), so the scorer distribution includes offensive rebounders and a second-chance branch. Defensive scheme changes which shot types are conceded in the first possession.
stages.distribution: Mixture over shot types with type-specific Bernoulli make probabilities, then a follow-up branch; yields a first-scorer pmf with a longer tail for bigs than their share of first shots suggests.

talent_strength.note: Shooter skill and team efficiency in the opening trips; because the race ends quickly, talent matters less than allocation.

opponent_matchup.note: Opening shot type and defence alignment.

role_personnel.note: Starting five and their first-shot shares.

availability_news.note: Late scratch and confirmation timing.

coaching_scheme.note: Scripted opening plays and play-calling.

environment.note: Altitude, arena and weather act through fatigue and shooting over a whole game; the first one or two possessions occur before fatigue accumulates, so no environmental input is justified for the first score.

game_context_script.note: Tip result and possession order set the race.

pace_volume.note: The first basket resolves within about three trips, so game-long pace (possessions per 48 minutes) changes the outcome distribution negligibly; nba.pace is audited WEAK and was removed from the stage lists.

efficiency_conversion.note: Make rate by first-shot type.

distribution_variance.note: Categorical pmf with small-sample uncertainty on shares.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Rest, back-to-back and playoff stakes alter minutes later in the game; the opening set is determined by the starting five and play script, and no evidence ties the schedule situation directly to who scores the first basket.

officiating_rules.note: Referee crew tendencies change free throws and fouls over the whole game, but a first basket occurs within the first minute, before foul patterns accumulate; the only rule-level item (whether FTs count) is a settlement-definition gap.

settlement_contract.note: No first-basket or first-team-to-score series is live in the ledger and rules text is absent, so what counts as the first basket (FT, tip-in, goaltend, own-basket credit) and what happens to a non-playing player is not verified; live series attached are overtime markets.

contract_review.settlement_definition: No first-basket-scorer or first-team-to-score series is live for NBA: after the market-universe reconciliation the ledger holds no series under this key (the overtime series KXNBAOT and KXNBASERIESOT that were misfiled here now sit under game_overtime_and_team_events). The target is therefore UNVERIFIED from Kalshi text: which scoring event counts (a made field goal only, or also a free throw), whether a non-starter who enters before the first score is eligible, how an own-basket credit, goaltending or basket-interference score resolves, what an inactive named player resolves to, and what a game cancelled before any score resolves to are all unknown. Sibling NBA game contracts use a 48-hour postponement window with a fair-price void, which is only an analogy here.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official play-by-play and box score of the game for the first made basket (or first scoring event, if free throws count); no live contract names its source.
variants_and_edge_cases: No live series: the reconciliation moved KXNBAOT and KXNBASERIESOT to game_overtime_and_team_events, so nothing under this key has rules or a title, and every stage below is conditional on a first-basket or first-team-to-score contract being listed.

Definition of 'first basket': whether a free throw counts, whether a tip-in, goaltend or basket-interference score counts, and whether a basket credited to a team after an opponent's own-basket counts as that team's first score are all unspecified because no first-basket contract text exists; a fair-price void for a game cancelled or postponed beyond 48 hours is only an analogy with the sibling game-level rule, not a settled term.
Player eligibility: sportsbook first-basket markets typically void a player who does not play; whether Kalshi uses fair price, No, or void for an inactive player is unverified.
A player who is not a starter can score first if he enters before the first made basket (early foul, injury), a rare event that makes the 'starters only' assumption approximate.

parlay_combo.label: NBA parlay / multi-leg combination markets
parlay_combo.target: Multiple game or player legs jointly resolving true (side, total, player prop legs)
parlay_combo.mechanism: A joint event across legs whose dependence matters: side and total correlate through team scoring, side and player props through blowout minutes, and several props of the same player through minutes. Pricing as a product of marginals misprices the joint, in either direction depending on the correlation sign. The joint distribution requires a game-level simulation tied to the players' minutes.

interactions.hypothesis: Favorite cover plus star over has negative dependence via minutes; underdog cover plus star over positive.
Team total up pushes all of a team's player overs up together; compute joint by simulation.
One injury news item is a common shock to all legs; correlated repricing creates arbitrage vs independent pricing.

The favourite-cover and star-over pair (for stars of either team) becomes negatively dependent through minutes only when the projected |expected margin| passes about 6-8 points, since starters of both teams sit only in lopsided games; below the threshold the two are close to independent.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate the correlation of cover and star-over indicators in expected margin buckets of 2 points and look for a knee.

interactions.hypothesis: A single pace shock lifts the game total and every player's counting stats, so total-over with two player overs has a high joint probability beyond the product; loadings determine how much.
interactions.how_to_test: Simulate with and without the pace factor and compare the joint to the product on historical games.

interactions.hypothesis: When a major teammate is ruled out, allocation shifts and the previously negative dependence between two remaining teammates' overs can turn less negative because both gain usage; the sign is conditional on the injury scenario.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate partial correlations separately in games with and without the major teammate.

interactions.hypothesis: The same injury news produces a void leg (player inactive) or a live leg with a minute limit; the combo rule on void legs switches the payoff structure, so the effective probability is regime-dependent.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute payoff probabilities under each void rule using historical status vintages and compare.

interactions.hypothesis: The correlation between margin and total is close to zero overall but positive for slow-paced underdog games and negative for fast-paced favourite runaways, so the joint is not a simple bivariate normal.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate the correlation within cells of pace and spread and test heterogeneity.

interactions.hypothesis: The pair's value is the product of the two title probabilities only while both teams are alive; once the NBA leg's team advances a round the pair's value rises proportionally, and any elimination is absorbing, so value moves as a function of the round reached in both leagues.
interactions.how_to_test: Track simulated pair values by round reached in each league on past seasons and compare them with the product of the two legs' round-conditional title probabilities.

interactions.hypothesis: A late scratch on one leg moves only that leg's win probability, but because the pack is a product, a drop from 0.65 to 0.50 on one leg cuts the 3-leg joint by 23% relative; status uncertainty on several legs compounds, so the joint's uncertainty band is much wider than any single leg's.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare pack probabilities computed at the morning injury report and at confirmed lineups and measure the change in Brier score of realised packs.

nonlinearities.shape: Hinge in |expected margin|: zero below about 6, strengthening above
nonlinearities.why: The minutes link between a cover leg and a star leg is zero until blowouts are plausible and then strengthens for starters of both teams (a function of |margin|), so the dependence cannot be a constant correlation; a side-signed expected margin feature would mis-specify it and only the usage effect should carry a side sign.

nonlinearities.shape: Tail dependence in the upper tail
nonlinearities.why: Hot-shooting nights lift all of a team's scorers at once, so joint overs have more mass in the extreme tail than a Gaussian copula with the same correlations.

nonlinearities.shape: Discrete non-Gaussian marginals
nonlinearities.why: Player counts at N+ thresholds are discrete with overdispersion; normal-score transformations must use the exact discrete CDF to avoid biasing joint probabilities.

mechanism_review.summary: A multi-leg combination resolves true only when all legs hold, so the probability is the joint probability of a vector of events, and the information needed is the dependence structure, not just the leg marginals. Same-game legs share latent factors: the margin (favourite covering moves the starters' minutes), the pace/total (more possessions raise all counting stats), team shooting luck (a hot night lifts all of a team's scorers together), and the injury/availability shock (one news item moves many legs). Within a team the allocation of points among players is a zero-sum split of a fixed team total, so two teammates' point overs are negatively associated at a given team score but positively associated through the team total. The joint is therefore best produced by a game-level simulation with explicit factors, not by pairwise correlations, and calibrated on historical box scores. Product-of-marginals pricing is biased: positive dependence makes joint hits more likely, negative makes them less likely, and the direction flips with leg type and team side. Three combinations are live and none is same-game: KXNBAPREPACK2ML/3ML are multi-game moneyline packs whose legs are separate games, so their probability is essentially the product of per-game win probabilities computed on one consistent information set, and KXNBANHL is a cross-league futures pair that is a product of two title probabilities with path-dependent early-No settlement. The same-game machinery (s1-s5) is retained for completeness but serves no live series.

stages.name: Leg marginals from their own mechanisms
stages.description: Each leg has its own generating process (a spread cover from the margin density, a total from pace and efficiency, a player stat from minutes and rates), and the joint can only be as good as these marginals. The marginals must be computed on the same information set and the same scenario weights for injuries, otherwise the dependence is applied to inconsistent inputs.
stages.distribution: Each marginal is a Bernoulli with probabilities from 0.05 to 0.95; leg probabilities combine multiplicatively under independence, which is the baseline to test against.

stages.name: Shared game-level latent factors
stages.description: Same-game legs load on a handful of common factors: the game total (pace times efficiency) moves every player's counting stats in the same direction; the margin moves starters' minutes and shot attempts together in favourites' blowouts; team-specific shooting luck lifts the team's scorers jointly. A factor model estimated on historical box scores gives the loadings by leg type and player role, and these loadings are what a simulation needs.
stages.distribution: Gaussian-like factor shocks with factor correlation near zero between margin and total (about 0.0-0.1) but strongly positive between total and any player points (loadings of 0.3-0.6).

stages.name: Minutes and blowout linkage
stages.description: The favourite-cover leg and a star-over leg are tied through minutes: a blowout lets the favourite cover but removes starters' late minutes on both sides, because the trailing coach also pulls starters. The minutes link is therefore a function of |expected margin| and is negative for both teams' stars against a favourite-cover leg; only the usage and score-state effect is side-specific (the trailing team's stars shoot more until pulled, the leader's share falls). The strength is a threshold in |expected margin|, not a constant: it appears only when the expected margin is large enough for starters to sit, and it is stronger for older stars and for coaches who pull early.
stages.distribution: Piecewise: near zero for expected margins below about 6, increasing in magnitude beyond for the minutes component (symmetric across sides); the usage component is side-specific and smaller. Sizes are recalled (u6).

stages.name: Within-team allocation and common shocks
stages.description: Given team points, individual points are a split, so overs on two teammates are negatively dependent conditional on the team total, while a single availability shock (a star ruled out) moves many legs at once and in different directions (the star's legs fail; teammates' usage legs rise). A game-level simulation that draws the injury scenario first, then team factors, then allocation preserves these dependencies.
stages.distribution: Dirichlet-multinomial-like allocation with negative within-team dependence of about -0.1 to -0.3; discrete scenario mixture for availability.

stages.name: Joint evaluation and void-leg settlement
stages.description: The final stage evaluates the joint probability from the simulation and applies the settlement rules for combos: if any leg can void (inactive player, protected exit, postponement), the payoff must be conditioned on the combination's rule, which changes the effective probability. Sampling error in the simulation and uncertainty in dependence parameters give interval estimates, not points, for the joint. Nested or implied legs are handled by evaluating every leg on the same simulated game draws (so implication holds exactly) rather than through a copula over marginals; whether such combinations may be listed is unknown (u5).
stages.distribution: Monte Carlo estimate with standard error sqrt(p(1-p)/n): about 0.5 percentage points at p = 0.5 and 10,000 draws, but only about 0.17 points (6% relative) at p = 3% and 0.07 points (14% relative) at p = 0.5%, so small joint probabilities need importance sampling or many more draws; dependence-parameter uncertainty adds comparable error.

stages.name: Cross-league title pair (live KXNBANHL)
stages.description: The live combo pays only if the named NBA team wins the title and the named NHL team wins the Stanley Cup. The NBA leg is a bracket simulation over seeds, series win probabilities and star health; the NHL leg comes from the NHL title model, which this NBA catalog does not own. Because the two leagues share no games, players or officials, the joint is the product of the two probabilities, and the early-No clause makes the price fall to zero at the first elimination of either team, so the path of both playoff runs (overlapping in April-June) and not only the end state matters for when the contract settles.
stages.distribution: Product of two small title probabilities (often 1-10% each, so the joint is usually below 1%); path-dependent with absorbing No states at each elimination round in either league.

stages.name: Multi-game moneyline packs (live KXNBAPREPACK2ML/3ML)
stages.description: Each pack leg is the named team winning its own game, so the joint is the product of per-game win probabilities, each built from availability-adjusted team ratings, home court and rest for that game. Because the games share no players, the only dependence is common information timing (late injury news on the same slate) and shared slate conditions, which are small; the main error source is compounding: three legs at 0.60 give 0.216, and a 0.03 error per leg moves the product by about 0.03 (15% relative). Leg probabilities must come from the own game model, not from listed moneylines.
stages.distribution: Product of 2-3 near-independent Bernoullis with leg probabilities 0.2-0.9; relative error grows with leg count; joint usually 0.05-0.5.

talent_strength.note: Leg marginals inherit talent from the single-leg mechanisms.

opponent_matchup.note: Matchup effects live inside each leg's marginal (opponent-adjusted rates for players, opponent defence for totals); the combination layer adds no matchup variable of its own beyond the dependence between legs.

role_personnel.note: Role determines how legs load on shared factors.

availability_news.note: A single availability item moves many legs and creates void states.

coaching_scheme.note: Pull timing creates the minutes link between margin and player legs.

environment.note: Venue, altitude and weather enter through each leg's own marginal; the combination layer has no environmental variable of its own beyond pace in the shared factors.

game_context_script.note: Blowout script links margin to minutes.

pace_volume.note: Pace and team totals as shared factors.

efficiency_conversion.note: Shooting efficiency is part of each leg's marginal; the correlated team shooting luck factor is carried by nba.game_factor_loadings, so no separate efficiency input is needed at the combo layer.

distribution_variance.note: Joint distribution and dependence.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Rest, back-to-back and late-season incentives change minutes for several legs simultaneously, but no combo-level input quantifies a rest-driven common shock; only each leg's own treatment exists.

officiating_rules.note: Crew tendencies affect foul and free-throw counts in individual legs; the combination layer inherits this through marginals, and no separate officiating variable is warranted for dependence.

settlement_contract.note: All three live series have rules text: multi-game moneyline packs (all named teams win their separate games; no void clause) and the cross-league title pair with early No. Same-game parlay rules do not exist (no series).

contract_review.settlement_definition: Three live series, all with recovered rules text. KXNBAPREPACK2ML and KXNBAPREPACK3ML are pre-packaged multi-game moneyline combos: Yes only if every named team wins its named game (sampled: two or three different Christmas Day 2025 games, each identified by its original schedule date). Their text has no secondary clause, so postponement, cancellation or a voided leg is not addressed. KXNBANHL is a cross-league championship pair: Yes if the named NBA team wins the 2026-27 NBA title and the named NHL team wins the 2026-27 Stanley Cup, and No as soon as either team is eliminated. No same-game player/team parlay series is live; stages s1-s5 describe that mechanism for completeness and do not serve a live series.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official final results of each named game (packs); official NBA Finals and Stanley Cup Final results and elimination events (KXNBANHL).
variants_and_edge_cases: Cross-league futures pair (KXNBANHL): two independent title races resolve within the same spring; the early-No clause means the contract can settle months before the second title is decided, and there are no void legs.

Void-leg treatment: the live pack texts have no postponement or cancellation clause, so whether a pack voids, drops the leg or resolves No when one game is postponed is not stated (u1); single-leg game markets use a 48-hour rule and fair-price void.

Cross-game versus same-game combos: the live packs (KXNBAPREPACK2ML/3ML) put legs in different games, where dependence is limited to shared information (same-day injury news, slate-wide officiating or rule effects) and is close to zero; same-game legs (not live) share margin, total, minutes and injury shocks.
Leg types mix half-point lines (no push) and integer N+ player thresholds (no push), but a whole-number sportsbook-style line could create a push leg whose handling inside a parlay is unseen.
Protected player legs (first-half-exit void) add a conditional-on-survival structure that interacts with other legs through the injury event.
Payoff is the product of marginals only under independence; pricing by the market maker embeds an assumed correlation that may differ from the true one.

Nested and logically implied legs: a spread cover implies the moneyline win, an N+ leg implies every lower N+ leg for the same player, and a PRA leg is a sum of its component legs, so such combinations have degenerate or perfect dependence that a Gaussian copula over marginals cannot represent; leg-count limits and whether nested legs are allowed are unknown.
Moneyline legs include overtime implicitly (NBA games cannot tie), so each pack leg is a plain win indicator with no push.

player_availability.label: NBA starting lineup / player availability
player_availability.target: Whether a player starts (or is in the starting lineup / is active)
player_availability.mechanism: A team decision made close to tip combining injury status, coach starting-lineup habits, rest policy and matchup. The best features are the report vintage and the player's calibrated resolution probability from similar status/team/rest contexts; confirmed starters appear ~30 minutes pre-tip, so markets closing earlier must carry a mixture. The info arrives in discrete bursts from official channels and reporters.
